body:
Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services Revised: 07/01/2026

Page 1 of 5

Breastfeeding: Breast Pump Issuance

Policy: Local agencies shall provide breast pumps to WIC clients when appropriate, along with appropriate education to directly support the initiation and continuation of breastfeeding.

Regulations: CFR 246.11 c, e, CFR 246.14 c (10), USDA FNS WIC Breastfeeding Policy and Guidance (July 2016), Colorado WIC Policy

Procedure/Additional Guidance: Breast pumps and breastfeeding aids that directly support the initiation and continuation of breastfeeding are an allowable WIC program cost. Research shows milk expression in the first few weeks postpartum, by hand or pump, can assist individuals in creating a good milk supply. However, it is important to note that breastfeeding directly at the breast provides many other benefits beyond that of only feeding breast milk by bottle. Additionally, providing pumps regardless of need may give clients the impression that special equipment is necessary to breastfeed, may contribute to feelings of inadequacy and lack of confidence, and may interfere with breastfeeding. ● Generally, pumps are issued to clients who are: ● Having difficulty establishing or maintaining an adequate milk supply due to maternal/infant illness; ● Parent/infant separation (e.g. hospitalization, return to work or school); and/or ● Parent temporary breastfeeding problems or medical need (e.g. severe engorgement). ● Pumps may not be issued to clients: ● As an inducement to consider or to continue breastfeeding. ● Prenatally to pregnant clients. ● Who are donating all their breast milk to a milk bank or other source. (To issue a pump, clients must be providing their own breast milk to their infant.) ● Liability: ● Staff providing breast pumps or aids must be adequately trained in lactation management (WLS, DBE, CLC, CLE, IBCLC) and/or in breast pump issuance procedures to provide clients with the appropriate information and follow-up. ● Clients must receive instruction from staff at the time of issuance on proper pump assembly, usage, cleaning, storage and maintenance. ● The Breast Pump/Aid Release Form must be reviewed with the client, and the client’s signature (or verbal acknowledgement) must be captured in the Compass computer system or on the printed form that must be uploaded into Compass. A print/electronic copy of the form must be offered to the client at the time of issuance. ● Local agency WIC Breastfeeding Coordinator will: ● Authorize and train local agency staff to appropriately assess and issue breast pumps to clients. ● Oversee breast pump inventory and order new breast pumps and accessories as needed from the State Office (see Breastfeeding: Breast Pump Ordering and Maintenance policy). ● Ensure all hospital-grade multi-user loaned breast pumps have a WIC asset tag adhered to the pump and are added to and tracked in the serialized inventory in Compass. ● Local agency staff must: ● Ask each client if they have received a breast pump or aid from another source (e.g., Medicaid, private insurance, health care provider, etc.). Options to obtain pumps and aids from Medicaid, health insurers, etc., should be considered before a pump or aid is provided through WIC. o If the client has a pump or aid from another source, WIC staff can provide education, support, and compatible pump supplies (e.g., breast shields/flanges) for its use. o WIC staff should limit issuing additional pumps or aids unless there is a need as determined by the staff’s clinical judgement. ● Assess each client needing/requesting a pump to determine the best pump for their situation. Breast pumps shall only be provided after a thorough breastfeeding assessment to ensure that a pump is the appropriate intervention. Assessments can be completed virtually, by phone, or in person. Staff may use the Breast Pump Questionnaire, as needed.

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services Revised: 07/01/2026

Page 2 of 5

● Document in Compass required client education (check boxes in Nutrition Education Covered and/or Care Plan) on: o The proper use, assembly/disassembly, cleaning, storage, and maintenance of the pump and associated collection kit/supplies issued; o Their responsibilities for handling and returning loaned, multi-user pumps. o Safe handling and storage of expressed breast milk. o Hand expression (to relieve normal engorgement and assist women in handling situations when they are without their infant and need to express milk - written materials and instructional videos are available). ● Review the Breast Pump/Aid Release Form with the client (virtually, by phone or in person) and capture the client’s signature or verbal acknowledgment in Compass to ensure the client accepts responsibility before accepting any type of pump. If a signature cannot be captured in Compass during an in-person appointment, upload a scanned copy of the signed Breast Pump/Aid Release Form into Compass. Provide the client with a copy of the Breast Pump/Aid Release Form that includes contact information for questions and the return date of loaned multi-user pumps, if applicable. The Breast Pump/Aid Release Form must be reviewed and a copy provided to the client each time any type of pump is issued. ● Document the type of pump issued and the reason for issuance in the Breastfeeding Equipment panel in Compass. ● Contact clients provided with any breast pump within 24-72 hours of issuance. Schedule a “Breast Pump Follow-up (remote)” appointment within this timeframe. During follow-up, answer questions, assess whether the initial issues/reasons for providing a pump have resolved, and provide referrals to lactation services or community support, as needed. o For clients with a loaned, multi-user pump, follow up at least monthly to assess ongoing need and provide lactation support. o Document all follow-up attempts in the Compass Scheduler using the “Breast Pump Follow- up (remote)” appointment type: ● If the client is reached, mark the appointment as “Seen” and complete a Care Plan, noting “Pump follow-up” in the Subjective section. ● If the client is not reached, mark the appointment as “No Show”. A Care Plan is not required. Marking as a “No Show” satisfies follow-up documentation requirements. o Note: Only one documented follow-up attempt is required per timeframe (24-72 hours for all pumps and monthly for multi-user pumps). Multiple contact attempts within the same month are not required. ● As best practice, refer a client requesting formula or an increase in formula after a pump is issued to the WIC High Risk Counselor who will assess the need for formula and follow the formula issuance guidance in the Breastfeeding: Definition, Promotion, Education and Support Standards policy.

*Note: Breastfeeding Peer Counselors (BFPC) not designated as WIC Lactation Specialists (WLS) cannot issue breast pumps and aids. BFPC should refer clients who may benefit from supplies or need assistance using supplies to appropriate staff (see Breastfeeding Scope of Practice policy). BFPC designated as WLS can only issue pumps and aids, as well as perform required pump follow-up contacts, to BFPC clients and must document contacts in the Client Care Plan.

Breast pumps and related pump supplies may only be purchased through the State Office ordering program. Only the additional breastfeeding supplies listed under the “Allowable Aids” indicated in the Breastfeeding: Breast Pump Ordering and Maintenance policy are allowed for purchase with WIC funding by local agencies. For breastfeeding aid issuance, see the Breastfeeding: Assistance, Aids and Contraindications policy.

Guidelines for Loaned Hospital-Grade Multi-User Electric Pumps Hospital-grade multi-user electric breast pumps are superior to single-user pumps because of a stronger motor, gentler suction options and capabilities that more closely mimic a baby at the breast for improved breast milk removal. Priority of hospital-grade multi-user pumps are provided to clients who have a medical need, whose infants have a medical need, or a breastfeeding challenge to maintain milk supply, including but not limited to: ● Infants with an ineffective suck or unable to breastfeed directly at the breast because of prematurity, respiratory or cardiac problems affecting endurance, and/or disorders of the oral or gastrointestinal structures. ● Latch on problems/breast rejection.

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services Revised: 07/01/2026

Page 3 of 5

● Severe feeding problems. ● Mastitis or breast infection. ● Mother on short-term medication(s) contraindicated for breastfeeding. ● Separation from infant (i.e., parent or infant hospitalized or ill) or mother is returning to work or school. ● Parent of multiples. ● Premature infant. ● Acute severe or recurrent engorgement not resolved with standard treatment (i.e., increased feedings, warm soaks, manual expression). ● Severely sore or cracked nipples. ● Abrupt weaning.

*Note: This list is not inclusive of all potential breastfeeding challenges and, therefore, the conditions for which a pump is loaned are left up to the decision of the local agency staff.

Issuance: Hospital-Grade Multi-User Electric Pumps Hospital-grade multi-user breast pumps should only be loaned to clients who have demonstrated reliability and can be located, if necessary. Multi-user breast pumps may only be issued in person and may not be mailed to clients. Multi-user breast pumps are prioritized for individuals with a medical need, and best practice is to issue a multi-user pump for the first 1-3 months, with the client’s expectation that a single-user pump would be issued, if needed, thereafter. In addition to the above requirements, staff must: ● Ask each client if they currently have a loaned multi-user breast pump from another source (e.g., Medicaid, private insurance, hospital loan, etc.). There should not be a need for an individual to have more than one multi-user loaned pump at one time. o If the client has a multi-user loaned pump from another source, WIC staff can provide education, support, and compatible pump supplies (e.g., breast shields/flanges) for the successful use of the pump. o WIC staff should limit issuing any additional pump while the client is loaning a multi-user pump from any source, unless there is a need determined by staff’s clinical judgement. ● At issuance, WIC staff shall inform participants that multi-user pumps are issued for temporary use to address specific breastfeeding or medical needs, such as resolving challenges or establishing milk supply. Participants must be advised that the pump should be returned once the need is resolved, typically within one to three months, and should transition to a single-user breast pump, if necessary. ● Complete the Breastfeeding Equipment panel. ● Review the Breast Pump/Aid Release Form with the client and document 2-3 individuals to contact in case the pump is not returned. ● Log each pump’s loan status, including the contact/return date, the date returned (once applicable) and at least two alternative contacts, including name and phone number or email address in Compass on the Breastfeeding Equipment panel. ● Inform clients that the double-pumping accessory/collection kits for the hospital-grade multi-user pump may not be loaned or shared with others, due to the possibility of cross-contamination. ● Use the Breastfeeding Equipment Due report in Compass to track loaned pumps. Pumps are visible on the report if the contact/return date is the current month or past due. ● Once a pump is returned, record the date returned and reason(s) for return (e.g., problem resolved) on the Breastfeeding Equipment panel. ● If a pump is kept longer than the expected return date, staff should follow up with the client, review the pump need and, if applicable, update the return date in Compass on the Breastfeeding Equipment panel and document follow-up in the Client Care Plan. ● Depending on the local agency inventory and because of the limited number of pumps, hospital-grade multi- user pumps used solely for medical problems or supply issues should be returned as soon as the need is resolved. If a pump is still necessary and a client qualifies, a single-user pump may be issued as a replacement (see qualifications below). ● Local agencies cannot withhold or deny WIC benefits or services from a client who has not returned a breast pump and/or not attended a pump follow-up appointment.

Clients with a loaned pump who transfer to another local WIC agency: ● Allow clients to have access to an electric pump when deemed necessary.

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services Revised: 07/01/2026

Page 4 of 5

● Preferred situation is for a mother to return the pump to the original clinic and staff work with the new clinic to quickly provide her with the same type of pump on arrival. ● If a mother transfers to a new clinic and does not return a loaned pump to the original clinic, the new clinic should exchange the pump with a pump from the new clinic and return the original pump, via transportation or mail, to the original clinic where it was issued.

Guidelines for Single-User Electric Pumps Single-user electric breast pumps are ideal for breastfeeding women who need help maintaining a milk supply and who have expressed genuine interest in breastfeeding exclusively for a goal of one year (use the WIC Breast Pump Questionnaire to aid in decision making). Single-user breast pumps may be provided in person or may be mailed via certified mail to clients. Primary reasons for issuing a single-user pump are: ● To help maintain adequate milk supply so that no formula is needed for the infant. ● To reduce the time and cost of WIC staff to follow up on loaned pumps for lower-risk situations.

*Note: This list is not inclusive of all reasons/needs for a single-user pump, therefore, the conditions for which a pump is loaned are left up to the decision of the local agency staff.

Single-user pumps are not as effective in removing milk as a hospital-grade electric pump due to weaker motors. Hospital-grade multi-user pumps are used to help establish and/or increase milk supply and are evidence-based ways to increase milk expression volume. This is one reason why WIC prefers clients already have a well-established milk supply before receiving a single-user pump.

While WIC strongly promotes exclusive breastfeeding for parents and children to receive the most benefits, WIC also understands and supports partial breastfeeding, as any breast milk is better than no breast milk.

Issuance: Single-User Electric Pumps Providing breast pumps to clients who do not need them may interfere with breastfeeding and result in unnecessary waste. Single-user pumps should only be provided to clients who: ● Have a well-established milk supply and are committed to continued breastfeeding. ● Are not receiving or have not received a single-user pump from another source (e.g., Medicaid, private insurance, health care provider, etc.). ● Are at least 4-6 weeks postpartum. (Supply is most effectively established in the first few weeks postpartum with the infant breastfeeding directly at the breast or by use of a hospital-grade multi-user loaned pump.) ● Are receiving an exclusive/fully breastfeeding food package, or the partially breastfeeding food package which has been individually tailored to meet the client’s needs. This is designed to provide for the supplemental nutrition needs of the breastfeeding pair, provide minimal formula supplementation to help mothers maintain milk production and provide incentives for continued breastfeeding by way of a larger variety and quantity of food. ● Are not currently borrowing a hospital-grade multi-user electric breast pump: o From WIC - Single-user pumps can be issued upon return of the loaned WIC pump. o From another source (e.g., Medicaid, private insurance, hospital rental, etc.) – Single-user pumps can be issued when the client states they have returned the loaned pump to the issuing agency, unless there is a need as determined by the WIC staff’s clinical judgement. ● Have a circumstance that warrants the issuance of a single-user pump, including: o Separation from infant(s) at least 6 consecutive hours on a regular basis (i.e., returning to work or school, custody sharing of the infant). o Parent of multiples. o Parent of infant(s) with physical or neurological impairment (i.e., weak suck, uncoordinated suck/swallow pattern, inability to suck, or inability to latch onto the breast). o Medical issue is resolved and the parent no longer needs hospital-grade pump, but is still interested in pumping on a regular basis for supply or separation from infant.

*Note: This list is not inclusive of all potential reasons for which a single-user pump can be issued and issuance is left up to the decision of the local agency staff.

In addition to the general pump issuance guidance above, staff must:

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services Revised: 07/01/2026

Page 5 of 5

● Encourage clients to save the breast pump for possible future infants. ● Not issue another single-user breast pump to a client for a future infant unless there are special circumstances warranting an exception to this guideline. The expectation is that a single-user pump can be used with all subsequent infants. Parents can receive additional collection kits and breastfeeding aids as needed with future WIC infants. ● Encourage clients to complete the manufacturer’s warranty registration. WIC clients are responsible for contacting the pump manufacturer themselves for repair or pump issues. ● Explain and remind WIC clients that single-user breast pumps are for one user only and should not be sold, lent to, or shared with others. Single-user pumps have an open motor system that cannot be removed, replaced or fully sterilized. When the client is finished with the single-user pump, it should be discarded or recycled by a pump manufacturer recycling program, not sold or given away. ● Label each single-user pump with a “not for resale” and “single-user only” statement (e.g., written in permanent marker on the bottom).

Guidelines for Manual/Hand Pumps Manual or hand breast pumps are ideal for breastfeeding clients who need a pump for convenience, short-term use, or to help alleviate a minor problem. If used regularly, manual pumps are typically not effective enough to maintain a client’s milk supply in the long term. Manual breast pumps may be provided in person or may be mailed via certified mail to clients. Reasons for issuing a manual pump include: ● Normal engorgement. ● Occasional separation from infant (e.g., meetings, social events). ● Working or in school with a flexible schedule and limited separation from the infant.

*Note: This list is not inclusive of all reasons/needs for a manual pump; therefore, the conditions for which a pump is loaned are left up to the decision of the local agency staff.

Formula Education When a breastfeeding client requests formula for her breastfed infant, staff must follow the formula procedures outlined in the Breastfeeding: Definition, Promotion, Education and Support Standards policy.

Loaning Breast Pumps to Partner Organizations If loaning/providing WIC breast pumps to partner organizations, a formal agreement must exist between the local agency and partner organization. See the Breastfeeding: Breast Pump Partnerships policy.

body:
Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services Revised: 03/01/2026 Page 1 of 3 Breastfeeding: Breast Pump Ordering and Maintenance Policy: Local agencies shall appropriately manage breast pumps provided to clients, including the ordering of pumps through the state purchasing program and maintaining breast pump inventories. Regulations: CFR 246.11 c, e, CFR 246.14 c (10), USDA FNS WIC Breastfeeding Policy and Guidance (July 2016), Colorado WIC Policy Procedure/Additional Guidance: Breast pumps and breastfeeding aids that directly support the initiation and continuation of breastfeeding are an allowable WIC program cost. Ordering ● Local agencies are responsible for maintaining an inventory of pumps and pump accessories, and for tracking items and quantities that need to be reordered. ● Breast pumps (multi-user, single-user, manual), collection kits and breastfeeding aids (e.g., breast shields/flanges, pump supplies) can only be ordered on a quarterly basis through a centralized process at the State WIC Program. o Local agency representatives complete the online Pump Order Form on or before the due date outlined in the reminder email sent to local agency pump representatives. o Each order requires the local agency WIC Director approval. o Pumps and pump accessories ordered are shipped directly to the local agency. o Local agency WIC funds cannot be used to purchase breast pumps or pump supplies, as purchasing such supplies outside of state ordering/contracts is not permitted. ● Other allowable breastfeeding aids may be purchased with funds available in the local agency budget (see the Breastfeeding: Assistance, Aids and Contraindications policy for allowable aids). ● Breast pumps and breastfeeding aids purchased with WIC funds should be provided at no cost to the client. ● Upon receipt, breast pumps and other items must be inspected for damage, ensuring the correct type and quantity ordered are received. ● After the type and quantity of ordered pumps and supplies are verified, local agency staff must send a confirmation of receipt to the State WIC Office fiscal officer. Tracking and Inventory ● Local agencies must maintain a serialized inventory of all hospital-grade multi-user loaned breast pumps in the Compass computer system. ● Upon receipt, each new pump must be added to the clinic’s inventory. Hospital-grade multi-user electric pumps must be added to the Serialized Inventory section in Compass under Operations. Enter the serial number provided by the pump manufacturer on the pump. ● All breast pumps must be kept in a locked cabinet or locked room at the clinic, and off the floor when not loaned. Electric breast pumps are costly, and careful attention must be given to maintaining, securing, and inventorying of all equipment. ● Hospital-grade multi-user electric loaned breast pumps must have an asset tag affixed to the pump for tracking purposes. The asset tag includes a unique identifying number and the State WIC telephone number. Asset tags are ordered through the State WIC Office fiscal office. ● Hospital-grade multi-user electric-loaded breast pumps must have a contact label securely affixed to each pump case stating who to contact if the pump is found. The WIC agency’s name, address, and telephone number should be included on the label (e.g., consider using mailing labels sealed with packing tape). ● Hospital-grade multi-user electric loaned breast pumps must have a Pump Cleaning Insert (available to order on the WIC materials order form) securely affixed to each pump case (via packing tape). ● Use the Breastfeeding Equipment Due report in Compass to track loaned pumps. Pumps are visible on the report if the due date/next contact date is the current month or past due. ● Once a pump is returned, record the date and reason(s) for return (e.g., problem resolved) on the Breastfeeding Equipment panel and Client Care Plan.

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services Revised: 03/01/2026 Page 2 of 3 ● If a pump is kept longer than the expected return date, staff should follow up with the client, review the pump need, and, if applicable, update the return date in Compass on the Breastfeeding Equipment panel and document follow-up in the Client Care Plan. Maintenance ● Loaned hospital-grade multi-user breast pumps and cases must be cleaned when returned to the clinic after being loaned to a client. Clean pumps as described by the manufacturer: o Ensure the pump is unplugged while cleaning. o Wear gloves. o Freshly mix the standard 1:10 bleach cleaning solution: 1 part bleach and 9 parts water. This solution is not stable and must be mixed fresh each day and discarded after use. o Apply the cleaning solution with a soft cloth to the pump and case. Leave the solution on for 30-60 seconds and rinse thoroughly with clean water using a soft cloth. ● If a pump is returned and contamination and/or insect infestation is suspected, do not re-issue the pump to another client and follow the instructions below under the Repair section. ● Loaned hospital-grade multi-user breast pumps must be checked for performance upon return and before reissuing to another client. Check pump functions properly and vacuum suction is adequate. ● All pumps must be stored in a secure, locked location and off the ground, away from electronic equipment, such as TVs, DVD players. Motors in electronic equipment can attract insects and could result in pump infestation. ● Educate on and ensure, upon issuance of all breast pumps, that each client understands proper cleaning and storage of breast pumps and supplies. Repair Multi-User Electric Breast Pumps ● If a hospital-grade multi-user electric breast pump needs repair or cleaning, contact the State WIC Office to verify warranty status. o Note: Warranty begins from the date of purchase and typically is a three year warranty. ● It is the responsibility of the local agency to track the repair and return of “warranty” pumps. ● Pumps Under Warranty – as deemed by the State WIC Office: o Contact the pump manufacturer's customer service by phone or email to request a warranty repair return authorization number and instructions. o Ship the pump, as instructed by the manufacturer to the factory for cleaning and repair. o Ship all pumps for repair without the cases. If a pump is believed to be contaminated or infested with insects, follow the manufacturer’s specific shipping instructions (manufacturers have specific instructions for shipping pumps contaminated or infested) and ship in the case. If a case is not returned by the manufacturer, the local agency may order a replacement case. ● Pumps Not Under Warranty: o Contact the State WIC Office fiscal unit to request prior approval for repair. A Purchase Request will need to be approved at the State level prior to contacting the pump manufacturer. o Upon approval from the State WIC Office, contact the pump manufacturer's customer service by phone or email to request a repair return authorization number. A request can be made at this time to provide an estimate of costs prior to work being completed. o Notify the State WIC Office fiscal unit upon receipt of the repaired pump. ● Pumps determined to be too damaged to repair or in need of disposal will be disposed of or recycled by the local agency. Check the pump manufacturer for recycling information and programs. Single-User Electric Breast Pumps ● It is the responsibility of the client to register the pump with the pump manufacturer and work with the pump manufacturer for warranty-related issues/pump malfunctions. It is not the WIC staff's responsibility to assist clients with the warranty process. WIC staff are not allowed to share client information with pump manufacturers, including the date of issuance, as it is a violation of data sharing/client privacy. o Note: Single-user breast pumps typically have the date of issuance to the client. Missing Pumps and Recovery* ● Hospital-grade multi-user electric breast pumps are costly and should be carefully maintained, tracked and secured. Such pumps should only be loaned to clients who have demonstrated they are reliable and who can be located, if necessary.

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services Revised: 03/01/2026 Page 3 of 3 ● WIC benefits cannot be denied to a client for failing to return a breast pump. If a loaned pump is not returned or cannot be located, staff should: o Attempt to reach the client and relatives/friends (contacts/referrals) listed on the Breastfeeding Equipment panel in Compass and/or Breast Pump/Aid Release Form. o Document all attempted contacts in Compass under Comments/Alerts of the client’s file. o Contact the State WIC Office with the pump serial number to obtain the depreciated value of the pump. ✔ If the missing pump is determined to have no monetary value (pump depreciated over 6 years), it is up to the agency/clinic to determine if pursuit of the pump should be continued. ✔ If the missing pump has a depreciated value near purchase price, it is cost effective for an agency/clinic to continue to pursue the missing pump. ● If contacts with the client are unsuccessful, send a certified letter to the client and attempt to call the client’s contacts listed in Compas and/or on the Breast Pump/Aid Release Form. Notify them if the pump is not returned promptly local authorities may be contacted. ● Depending on the pump’s depreciated value, the agency/clinic can determine whether to request assistance from local law enforcement. However, not all local law enforcement will act on requests for assistance. ● If the pump’s depreciated value is still at or near purchase price and cannot be recovered, contact the State WIC Office for further instructions. ● If the pump is not returned, the client may not be eligible for a breast pump (loaned or single-user) in the future. *Note: Breast pumps are a WIC benefit and it is a participant violation if a client is found to sell or offer to sell WIC breast pumps - see Participant Violation policy for full details.

body:
Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services Revised: 07/01/2026

Page 1 of 2

Breastfeeding: Breast Pump Partnerships

Policy: Local agencies may formally partner with community organizations to ensure WIC clients have easy access to breast pumps and related pump supplies.

Regulations: CFR 246.11 c, e, CFR 246.14 c (10), USDA FNS WIC Breastfeeding Policy and Guidance (July 2016), Colorado WIC Policy

Procedure/Additional Guidance: Breast pumps and breastfeeding aids that directly support the initiation and continuation of breastfeeding are an allowable WIC cost. Partnering with community organizations to provide WIC breast pumps assists in providing early and easy access to pumps for WIC clients. This can help WIC clients to initiate and maintain breastfeeding, increasing the likelihood both parent and child receive health benefits associated with breastfeeding. Partner organizations include, but are not limited to: hospitals, health care provider clinics, local public health agency programs (e.g., Nurse Family Partnership).

Requirements ● A formal written agreement between the local WIC agency and partner organization must be in place (see below), reviewed and dated by both parties annually, and renewed with new signatures from both parties at least every two or three years, as indicated in the written agreement. ● WIC breast pumps may only be provided to individuals verified to be currently active on WIC (see below) and are eligible to receive a pump. ● WIC breast pumps cannot be issued to clients prenatally. ● A completed and signed Breast Pump/Aid Release Form must be provided to the local WIC agency for every pump issued to WIC clients for documentation purposes (recorded/uploaded into Compass). If issuing a multi-user loaned pump, the partner organization must obtain 2-3 individual contacts from the WIC client to be used if the pump is not returned. ● Information must be provided by the partner on proper assembly, usage, cleaning and maintenance of the pump and related supplies, as well as proper breast milk storage and who to contact for support. ● Multi-user breast pumps may be loaned to partner organizations to provide to verified WIC clients in- person, as deemed necessary for multi-user breast pump issuance within the Breastfeeding: Breast Pump Issuance policy. ● Single-user and manual breast pumps may be provided to partner organizations to give to verified WIC clients, as deemed necessary based on the issuance guidance within the Breastfeeding: Breast Pump Issuance policy. ● Either party can terminate the agreement at any time and request the pumps and related supplies be returned to the local WIC agency as soon as possible.

Formal Written Agreement In order for a partner organization to provide WIC pumps, the local WIC agency must create a formal written agreement renewed every two or three years, as indicated in the agreement, that is signed by both the local agency director and partner organization detailing the required procedures and requirements. Such documents may be in a memorandum of understanding (MOU), memorandum of agreement (MOA), interagency agreements, specialty services agreements, etc. The written agreement must contain: ● Full contact information for the local WIC agency and the partner organization. ● Purpose of the agreement and effective dates (start and end dates – must not exceed three years in length - and annual review dates). ● Responsibilities of each party in the agreement should include, but are not limited to: o How the partner organization obtains pumps, associated collection kits, etc., from the local WIC agency. o How the pumps will be stored in a secure location at the partner organization. o How the partner organization verifies the individual is currently active on WIC (see below) and is eligible to receive a pump. o A prohibition on issuing WIC breast pumps prenatally.

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services Revised: 07/01/2026

Page 2 of 2

o Required duties the partner organization must complete when issuing a pump (e.g., Breast Pump Release Form signatures, using and maintaining/cleaning the pump, human milk storage, etc.). o Communication requirements between the local WIC agency and partner organization. o Client follow-up responsibilities after a pump is issued. ● Make and model of the pumps provided to the partner organization. ● Serial numbers of the pumps provided to the partner organization (optional - if designated pumps are assigned for the partner organization’s specific use). ● Signatures of both parties.

The local WIC agency must inform the State Office Nutrition Consultant and State Breastfeeding Coordinator and provide a copy of the signed agreement. The agreement must be reviewed annually and renewed every two or three years (with new signatures and dates) by both parties. If loaning multi-user breast pumps to the partner organization, the pumps issued must: ● Be in the local WIC agency’s serialized inventory in Compass; ● Have a WIC asset tag affixed to the pump; ● Have WIC contact information written on/affixed to the pump; ● Have a cleaning insert adhered to the inside of the pump case; and ● The local agency must document the serial numbers of the specific pumps loaned to the partner organizations and track the pumps.

WIC Client Verification For a partner organization to issue a breast pump, they must first verify the individual is currently an active WIC client. Due to data-sharing restrictions in place to protect and respect the privacy of clients, WIC staff may not provide information on individual clients to partner organizations. WIC clients can provide verification of their current WIC status to share with the partner organization by: ● Calling their WIC agency in the presence of the partner organization and requesting WIC staff to share their current WIC status; ● Showing the partner organization their current benefits available via the WICShopper; and/or ● Provide a printed copy of the verification of enrollment that the client obtained previously from WIC staff.

body:
Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section: Nutrition Services Revised: 03/01/2026 Page 1 of 4

Breastfeeding: Definition, Promotion, Education and Support Standards Policy: Local agencies shall provide breastfeeding promotion, education and support to participants and designate a Local Agency Breastfeeding Coordinator. Regulations: CFR 246.11 c(2),(5),(7)(i)-(iv), CFR 246.2, CFR 246.10 e, USDA FNS WIC Breastfeeding Policy and Guidance (July 2016), Colorado WIC Policy Definitions: Breastfeeding Recommendations: Human milk is the optimal food for infant growth and development. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends exclusively breastfeeding for the first 6 months after birth, and supports continued breastfeeding for 2 years or as long as desired. Exclusive Breastfeeding: An infant does not receive any additional foods or fluids other than breast milk unless medically recommended. Breastfeeding Woman: Refers to women up to one year postpartum who are providing their breast milk to their own infant(s), including: ● Women who are providing any amount of breast milk to their infant(s) via breastfeeding (exclusively or partially). ● Women who are providing any amount of breast milk to their infant(s) by expressing the breast milk by hand or pump and feeding the expressed breast milk to the infant. ● Women who are providing any amount of breast milk to infant(s) to whom they did not give birth and for whom she has legal responsibility. Examples include foster mothers, adoptive mothers, and female partners in the same household. A non-birth breastfeeding woman may receive WIC services if she meets eligibility criteria and the infant receiving her breast milk is a WIC participant. Breastfeeding Descriptions Definitions*: • Exclusively Breastfeeding (“Excl BF”): Infant fed only human milk, vitamins, minerals, and/or medications. Infant receives no food package from WIC. • Primarily Exclusive/No Food Pkg (“Prim Excl/No F Pkg”): Infant fed something other than human milk, vitamins, minerals, and/or medications on rare occasions, or has received a limited-time (not routine) feeding of infant formula, human milk fortifier, cow’s milk, juice, sugar water, rehydration solution, baby food, or anything else. Includes infants whose exclusive breastfeeding is interrupted because of special circumstances, such as acute illness, hospitalization, or caregiver misinformation. Infant receives no food package (no infant formula) from WIC. • Primarily Exclusive/Complimentary Foods (“Prim Excl/Comp”): Infant fed any complimentary food in addition to only being fed human milk, vitamins, minerals, and/or medications. These complimentary foods are provided on a routine or ongoing basis, regardless of the amount. Infant receives age- appropriate food packages with no WIC infant formula. • Partially Breastfeeding In Range (“Part BF – in range”): Infant fed human milk and something other than human milk, such as complementary foods, infant formula (non-WIC supplied or from WIC up to the maximum provided for a mostly breastfeeding infant - described in Table 1 of 7 CFR 246.10). • Partially Breastfeeding Out of Range (“Part BF Woman – out of range”): Infant fed human milk and receives more than the maximum amount of infant formula from WIC provided for a mostly breastfeeding infant, but less than the amount provided for a non-breastfeeding infant. • No Longer Breastfeeding (“No Longer BF”): Infant was breastfeeding at some point in time, but has now discontinued. • Never Breastfed (“Never BF”): Infant was never breastfed. Should only be used if breastfeed was never initiated. • Breastfeeding Child (“BF Child”): Child greater than or equal to 12 months of age continuing to receive human milk.

*Note: does not include clients providing breast milk to infants only by donating their breast milk to a milk bank or other source.

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section: Nutrition Services Revised: 03/01/2026 Page 2 of 4 Procedure/Additional Guidance: Promotion of Breastfeeding Colorado WIC will promote and support breastfeeding. ● Each local agency program will designate a staff person to serve as the Breastfeeding Coordinator to provide leadership to the local WIC agency on breastfeeding promotion, education and support matters. ● All agency staff exhibits a positive attitude toward breastfeeding and, depending on their position, be expected to encourage, educate on, promote and support breastfeeding and make referrals for breastfeeding services beyond WIC. See Breastfeeding Roles in Colorado WIC Clinic in the Breastfeeding: Scope of Practice policy. Staff Training Federal regulations require local agency staff to have a basic knowledge of breastfeeding and understand their unique role in supporting breastfeeding as the standard method of infant feeding. All staff have a valuable role in supporting breastfeeding women in WIC. ● The local agency Breastfeeding Coordinator helps train staff in the provision of breastfeeding support services and serves as a mentor for new and existing staff. ● All new staff must complete at a minimum the online WIC Lactation Specialist (WLS) training series Modules 1-3, as well as additional task-appropriate breastfeeding training as determined by the local agency Director and/or Breastfeeding Coordinator. ● State office will provide in-service training and technical assistance on the promotion and management of breastfeeding to staff at local agencies. Clinic Environment All local agencies must develop policies and create a clinic environment that endorses breastfeeding as the preferred method of infant feeding. A positive breastfeeding clinic environment demonstrates to mothers the importance WIC places on breastfeeding and enhances staff efforts in promoting breastfeeding. ● Encourage staff to communicate a positive attitude toward breastfeeding. ● All printed materials (e.g., handouts, pamphlets, posters), audiovisual materials and social media messages used will use positive breastfeeding messages and images and be free of infant formula product names or manufacturer information or logos. ● Ensure infant formula, bottles, feeding supplies and related materials are out of the sight of participants and the public. ● Office supplies (e.g., cups, calendars, pens, note pads, etc.) must be free of infant formula product and manufacturer/sponsor names and information. ● Refuse free gifts and samples from infant formula representatives for use by local agency staff. ● Encourage and support local agency staff to breastfeed their children. ● Support breastfeeding in clinics and provide private space (other than a toilet stall) for staff and participants to breastfeed and/or express breast milk. ● Develop a mechanism to incorporate positive peer influence into the clinic. This could include a breastfeeding affirmation bulletin board where pictures and statements from breastfeeding moms and infants are displayed (from staff and participants), and/or classes or support groups where breastfeeding women and/or peer counselors talk to pregnant women. Education and Support Breastfeeding education and support are provided throughout the prenatal and postpartum period, particularly at critical times when the mother is most likely to need assistance. All women should be educated on the benefits of exclusive breastfeeding. Prenatal Education Prenatal education and breastfeeding intention prior to delivery is one of the best predictors of a woman’s breastfeeding success. Every opportunity should be taken during a woman’s pregnancy to educate on the importance of breastfeeding, address breastfeeding concerns and questions, and provide encouragement to initiate and continue breastfeeding as long as possible. • The local agency will use prenatal breastfeeding education protocols which: ✔ Integrate breastfeeding promotion into the continuum of prenatal nutrition education. ✔ Include an assessment of participant knowledge, concerns, attitudes and support networks related to breastfeeding.

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section: Nutrition Services Revised: 03/01/2026 Page 3 of 4 ✔ Provide initial and follow-up breastfeeding education sessions to each participant and include breastfeeding education at every prenatal participant visit and interaction. ✔ Are comprehensive, up-to-date, and culturally appropriate. ✔ Include information on the benefits of exclusive breastfeeding and practical strategies to combat potential challenges. ✔ Include information to prepare mothers to communicate effectively with hospital staff of her decision to breastfeed. ✔ Include information to prepare mothers to communicate effectively with her employer/school as she prepares for maternity leave. • Staff must invite all pregnant women to a breastfeeding/infant feeding class or provide comparable education one-on-one with participants. • Staff will follow local agency systems in place to refer pregnant women to the Breastfeeding Peer Counseling program. Postpartum Education The first few weeks postpartum are critical time periods in helping mothers build a milk supply and confidence. Research shows mothers with early and continued breastfeeding support are the most likely to succeed and breastfeed for longer durations. • Staff will make efforts to schedule mothers who intend to breastfeed for subsequent certification as soon after delivery as possible in order to provide timely breastfeeding support. • Inform participants that WIC helps mothers establish a successful breastfeeding relationship with their infant(s) and provides support to build their milk supply. • All postpartum contacts provide positive reinforcement for the continuation of breastfeeding. • Staff will document a mother’s plan for breastfeeding in her nutrition education record and provide education and support to help her achieve her breastfeeding goals. • Staff will develop a plan to assure that women have access to locally available support programs/services early in the postpartum period (when infant is 0-2 weeks of age). • Local agencies will invite women to a WIC support group or refer women to a community breastfeeding support group. • Staff will provide and/or identify education and support services for breastfeeding women returning to work or school. • Local agencies collaborate with other programs/groups that provide breastfeeding education/support. • Staff will follow local agency systems in place to refer new mothers and breastfeeding women to the Breastfeeding Peer Counseling program. Formula When a breastfeeding woman requests formula for her breastfed infant, the first priority is to help the woman achieve her breastfeeding goals. Staff must: ● Perform a nutrition assessment and use participant centered approaches to understand each mother’s individual request for formula supplementation and determine the appropriateness of supplementation. ● Ask open-ended questions to understand the reasons behind the infant formula request and assess a mother’s understanding of the potential impact of formula on milk supply and breastfeeding. ● Continue to affirm, encourage and support any amount of breastfeeding. ● Inform the mother that her food package will change based upon how much she is breastfeeding. ● Document a mother’s plan for breastfeeding, formula use and education provided in her nutrition education record. ● When formula is issued to a breastfed infant: o Provide only the minimum amount to meet, but not exceed the infant’s nutritional needs. Remember that WIC is a supplemental program and mothers will have greater breastfeeding success if they continue to breastfeed and/or express their milk regularly. o Provide powdered formula as a supplement because it can be prepared in as small a quantity as needed. o Determine the amount of supplement necessary that meets but does not exceed the infant’s nutritional needs and assign the appropriate food package. A breastfeeding infant who receives any formula from WIC is no longer in the fully breastfeeding category and needs to be adjusted

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section: Nutrition Services Revised: 03/01/2026 Page 4 of 4 appropriately. o Adjust the mother’s food package appropriately based upon her level of breastfeeding and amount of infant formula issued. A woman over six months postpartum and determined to be in the “some breastfeeding” category will not receive a food package, however can still receive all other WIC services. o Document appropriately in the Compass computer system. o Provide regular follow up with the mother at least monthly to continue to support breastfeeding success as able. Banked Human Milk Banked human milk is not a WIC-eligible supplemental food (as defined by 7 CFR 246.10) and WIC federal funds cannot be used for the purposes of collecting, storing, purchasing, or disseminating banked human milk. WIC staff may inform parents about banked human milk, refer clients to human milk banks, and inform parents about donating their milk. Additionally, WIC clinics can serve as a human milk depot in partnership with another organization/human milk bank. Prior to serving as a milk depot, a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) is required between the WIC agency and human milk bank/organization to clearly define the roles and responsibilities of each organization and explicitly state that banked human milk is not a WIC benefit, nor is the milk depot sponsored by WIC.

body:
Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section: Nutrition Services Revised: 06/01/2025

Page 1 of 1

Breastfeeding: Human Milk Fortifier

Policy: Local agencies may issue human milk fortifier (HMF) to participants with proper medical documentation to promote and support continued breastfeeding.

Regulations: CFR 246, 79 FR 12273 C (5)(f), USDA FNS WIC Breastfeeding Policy and Guidance (July 2016), Colorado WIC Policy

Procedure/Additional Guidance: Human milk fortifier (HMF) is predominantly a protein and mineral supplement, that when added to human milk boosts the calories and nutrition to better meet the needs of very premature infants. Studies have shown the addition of HMF is associated with improved growth, bone mineralization and neurologic outcomes. HMF is initiated in the hospital and may be maintained after discharge with proper medical oversight and documentation. • HMF is classified as an exempt infant formula by USDA. • For clients with Medicaid insurance, WIC staff should refer to a Medicaid Durable Medical Equipment (DME) provider to obtain requested HMF. Medicaid is the first payer for HMF in Colorado. • For clients who do not have Medicaid insurance, issuance of HMF through WIC is allowed with monthly authorization by the infant’s health care provider (provided on the Physician Authorization Form – PAF). • WIC participant must have access to a breast pump (either from or outside of WIC). • WIC participant must be provided with breastfeeding support and continued, regular follow up (ideally weekly). • Breastfeeding definition guidance: o If receiving HMF not from WIC (from other sources only – e.g., Medicaid):  If the infant is not receiving any HMF/formula from WIC, the infant's BF Description can be “Prim Excl/No Food Package”. The infant must be marked as receiving something other than breast milk and marked as receiving formula rarely (record the date HMF or any formula was started) in the nutrition interview. Choosing rarely to formula (while not entirely accurate) will allow for correct data collection of HMF start date and allow a fully breastfeeding food package to be issued. Add HMF issuance in the notes/care plan in Compass.  Mother may be considered fully breastfeeding and receive the appropriate food package. o If receiving HMF from WIC:  Since USDA classifies HMF as formula, the infant must receive a Breastfeeding Description of “Part BF” and be marked as receiving formula regularly in the nutrition interview.  The mom's food package is based on the infant's BF Description. Therefore, mom will get a Part BF Food Package.  Once HMF from WIC is discontinued, the infant’s BF Description can be changed to “Prim Excl/No Food Package” and the mother can be transitioned back to the fully breastfeeding package. • Infant must be monitored closely by their health care provider (thus require monthly PAF submitted). • HMF is most often discontinued prior to discharge and is not necessary or healthy to receive on a long-term basis. HMF must discontinue once the infant is 12 weeks post-discharge from the hospital or as indicated by the health care provider. • HMF cannot be reconstituted/fed on its own as an infant formula to provide proper nutrition, it must be added to human milk. • HMF cannot be added to formula or used in conjunction with formula “sprinkles” to fortify human milk. HMF is the preferred source of fortification for human milk as research indicates fortification of human milk with formula is inferior nutritionally to HMF. • HMF cannot be issued with other infant formula. HMF is authorized for use when a mother is, or is attempting to be, exclusively breastfeeding.

For questions or more information, refer to the Colorado Guidelines for Health Care Professionals for Human Milk Fortifier after NICU Discharge (plus mixing instructions) available on the Colorado WIC website.

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services Revised: 01.01.2023

Page 1 of 2

Breastfeeding: Scope of Practice

Policy: WIC regulations require the roles and responsibilities be defined for all staff in the support and promotion of breastfeeding.

Regulations: CFR 246.3e, USDA FNS WIC Breastfeeding Policy and Guidance (July 2016), Colorado WIC Policy

Procedure/Additional Guidance: The core competencies of staff as defined by USDA include: • Recognize own beliefs and attitudes regarding breastfeeding and the impact of those beliefs and attitudes on WIC participant decisions. • Know the benefits of breastfeeding for infants, mothers, families, community and environment, and apply to daily clinic activities. • Self-identify as part of the WIC “Team” that promotes, protects and supports breastfeeding. • Understand how the WIC food packages for the breastfeeding dyad support breastfeeding. • Understand how to assist mothers to overcome common barriers to initiation of, exclusive and continued breastfeeding. • Develop rapport and foster open dialogue to successfully communicate with pregnant women and mothers. • Identify factors that can impact breastfeeding during the prenatal assessment process. • Identify physiological factors that impact breastfeeding. • Understand optimal breastfeeding practices that help mothers initiate and maintain breastfeeding. • Recognize common breastfeeding concerns and protocols for obtaining additional assistance for mothers. • Assist women who are employed or in school with tailored strategies for continuing to breastfeed after returning to work or school. • Apply knowledge of lactation to supporting breastfeeding in varied situations. • Understand the role of clinic and community support for breastfeeding. • Collaborate with other programs/groups that provide breastfeeding education and support in the community.

Staff Training • Staff can receive breastfeeding education to meet the above core competencies by completing the Level II Colorado WIC Breastfeeding Module. • Staff can become WIC Lactation Specialists (WLS) [and/or Designated Breastfeeding Experts (DBE)] by attending a Colorado WIC training specifically designed to equip staff with knowledge to counsel women and infants with nutrition risk factors (NRFs) related to breastfeeding complications (NRFs 602 & 603). • All WIC Directors and High Risk Counselors are required to have advanced lactation training by becoming a WLS (by attending the training and passing the exam within one year of hire), DBE, and/or obtaining advanced lactation credentials (e.g., Certified Lactation Counselors (CLC), Certified Lactation Educators (CLE), International Board Certified Lactation Consultants (IBCLC)). • Educators are invited to participate in WLS trainings and must successfully pass the exam and observations of participant interactions to become WLS and perform initial counseling on high risk breastfeeding complications. • Breastfeeding peer counselors (BFPCs) with at least 12 months of work experience, or per the discretion of the LA BFPC Coordinator, may participate in WLS trainings and must successfully pass the exam and observations of participant interactions to become WLS. • Staff who have advanced lactation credentials are not required, but recommended, to attend the WLS training, regardless of their WIC title. Observations of participant interactions are not required.

The table on the following page defines general roles which staff with various training, education and credentialing can practice.

*Note: WIC agencies with staff who are RN, IBCLCs and who also perform public health nursing positions which require greater technical expertise may have expanded scope of practice beyond that described in this policy.

body:
Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services Revised: 07/01/2026 Page 1 of 2 Education Documentation Policy: A minimum of two nutrition education contacts must be documented in the participant’s WIC record for each 6-month certification period. For breastfeeding women, infants and children certified for more than six months, contacts must be offered on a quarterly basis. Actively participating breastfeeding women of an infant older than 6 months of age receiving out of range formula do not receive food benefits but a nutrition education contact is still required. Regulation: 7 CFR 246.11(e) Procedure/Additional Guidance: The purpose of documentation is to record information provided to and from the participant during a WIC visit. Quality documentation ensures continuity of care and enables staff to review plans from previous visits, follow up on participant goals, and reinforce nutrition education messages. Participant Care Plan information must be entered no more than 10 days after a visit. The following are required components of nutrition education documentation in Compass: ● Completion of the Nutrition Education panel including: o Selecting Nutrition Education Topics Covered, o Documenting any pamphlets provided in the Pamphlets Provided field, o Checking the High Risk Follow Up Appointment check box if a high risk visit is performed by the high risk WIC counselor or IBCLC/CLC. ● Completion of the Participant Care Plan including: o Participant comments, objective information, assessment, nutrition education, pamphlets, goals, referral and follow-up plan as appropriate and as described below. o At least one goal the participant identified documented (exception, low-risk participants who complete a wichealth.org lesson or those that complete a nutrition education contact via a Nutrition Education class). Documenting High Risk: When a WIC educator identifies a participant to be high risk and the WIC High Risk Counselor provides high risk counseling that day, both WIC staff enter a separate education note. Only one education note is required when the WIC High Risk Counselor completes both the certification/recertification/follow up and high risk counseling in one visit. Documenting Group Education: In order for a group education session to be counted as a nutrition contact, a class outline must be on file that specifies the topics covered, materials used, and the class title. Nutrition education class topics are chosen when a class is created in the Compass scheduler. When a parti cipant completes a class, those topics are transferred to their nutrition education record. A care plan is not required. Creating A Care Plan: The Care Plan – Participant panel is where all subjective, objective, assessment, counseling and plan, goals and referral information is located. Here are lists of possible items within each section: ● Subjective: is information obtained directly from the participant, the participant's family, or a healthcare professional. ✔ Participant comments will pull into the Subjective area from the text boxes in the current Nutrition Interview. ✔ Staff may add additional information in the white text box under Subjective such as: o Additional participant comments related to: medical, growth and iron, nutrition practices, lifestyle and/or personal factors. o Reason why a staff-assigned risk factor was assigned. o Other needs identified. o Comments related to follow up on previous goals. o Comments related to follow up on previous referrals. o Additional subjective information that was not collected during the Nutrition Interview can be added to the open text boxes.

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services Revised: 07/01/2026 ✔ Objective: is information from measurable facts such as a tests, physical measurements, etc. Participant information such as category, age, blood work, height, weight, week’s gestation, and growth percentile data entered in previous Compass panels will pull into the objective area of the care plan. Additional objective information such as special dietary needs, special formulas, and tailored food packages can be added to the open text boxes. ● Assessment: ✔ Compass risk factors added in previous Compass panels will pull into the assessment area of the Care Plan. In the white text box under Assessment, WIC staff members may add their assessment. An example of an assessment would be “diet high in sugar sweetened beverages” or “participant has gained x amount of weight in x days/weeks.” Agencies that use the Nutrition Care Process, (Problem, Etiology & Signs/Symptoms) PES statements may be added here also. Staff are not required to write an assessment, but may do so if they choose. ● Counseling/Plan/Pamphlets: ✔ Selected counseling topics and pamphlets from the Nutrition Education Panel automatically populate into these text boxes when a new Participant Care Plan is selected. ● Counseling/Education: ✔ Additional counseling and nutrition education information can be entered into the text box to clarify or enhance the topics and counseling points entered in the Nutrition Education Panel. ● Goals: ✔ What the participant states will be their next step or what they will work on or do (based on their stage of change). ✔ One goal is required and should be participant centered, specific and time sensitive. ● Referrals: ✔ Each agency has a list of organizations that is entered into Compass for outreach and referral purposes. Referrals provided to participants are pulled from those documented on the Referral- Participant panel in the Family/Intake area of Compass. ● Plan: The plan is a place to record information to be covered at the next visit or additional measures to take. A plan is entered for future visits such as a referral to the WIC High Risk Counselor, the items that need to be completed for the next visit or additional referrals. If applicable, the WIC High Risk Counselors should enter when to schedule the next high risk visit with the WIC High Risk Counselor. Elements of Quality Nutrition Services Documentation: Consistent: Follows protocols set by Colorado WIC Clear: Precisely stated and easily understood by any reader Organized: Follows a logical order that minimizes duplication Complete: Creates a picture of the participant, the services provided over time, and outlines a plan for future services Concise: Contains relevant information Documentation of Other Contacts: WIC staff should document other visits or contacts in the participant’s care plan when education or information is exchanged or goals are set. Note: For appointments such as the Anthro/Hgb Only appointment, where staff are only gathering height, weight or hemoglobin (either in-person or remotely) and no information is exchanged, staff do not need to create a Care Plan. Editing WIC Records: A participant care plan cannot be edited more than 3 days after it was created. If more information needs to be entered in Compass for a participant after 3 days, a new education note must be created. In this case you would not need to enter a new record in the Nutrition Education panel as you have already created a nutrition education contact for this visit. Create a new record in the Participant Care Plan panel and note the date of the original education note in the new note. Page 2 of 2

body:
Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services

Revised: 04/01/2025

Page 1 of 6

Food Packages - Infants

Policy: WIC staff shall select infant’s food packages according to the infant’s age, breastfeeding status (Excl BF, Prim Excl/No F Pkg, Prim Excl/Comp, Part BF, No Longer BF, and Never BF), and nutritional needs.

Regulation: 7 CFR 246.10, Policy Memodandum #2025-3

Procedure/Additional Guidance: When certifying/recertifying a mother/infant pair, begin with entering infant data into Compass and then proceed with entering the mother’s data. WIC food packages can be promoted to incentivize and support clients to reach their breastfeeding goals. When appropriate, refer to local agency staff with advanced breastfeeding credentials to provide breastfeeding assessment and support.

Food Package Types/Categories for Infants:  Exclusively Breastfeed Infants: An infant who is breastfed and receives no WIC formula.  Fully Formula Fed or “Full Formula”: An infant who receives WIC formula and is not breastfed.  Partially (Mostly) Breasfeeding Infant: An infant who is breastfed and receiving WIC formula.  “Partial (Mostly) BF Within Range”: An amount of standard formula an infant can receive that allows mother to receive a partially breastfeeding food package for herself.  “Partial BF Out of Range”: An amount of standard formula greater than what is allowed for mother to receive a partially breastfeeding food package for herself.

Infant Food Packages There are three food package options:  Exclusively breastfed  No food package is needed for the infant until he/she is 6 months old. The mother should receive either a model or tailored food package appropriate for an exclusively breastfeeding woman.  Partially Breasfeeding Infant  If the mother reports that she is breastfeeding and offering or requesting formula, first ask open- ended questions to determine why formula is being used or requested and find out what the mother’s breastfeeding plan or goal is. Affirm the mother for breastfeeding. Depending on the situation, counseling may be done by the educator or can be passed on to a High Risk Counselor, WLS, or DBE. Discuss with the mother the alternatives to formula, such as breast milk collected by hand or breast pump. If, after counseling and education, the mother requests formula, verify that the infant’s breastfeeding description is “part BF” and provide only the minimum amount of formula needed to meet, but not exceed the nutritional needs of the infant. Reinforce the importance and benefits of any amount of breastfeeding. Remember that mothers have greater breastfeeding success when they continue to breastfeed and/or express breast milk regularly. The amount of formula the infant receives determines the mother’s food package. Explain that food packages with smaller amounts of formula may enable her to receive more food for herself.  Fully Formula Fed  A fully formula-fed infant receives a formula food package and the mother receives a food package for postpartum/non breastfeeding women until her infant is 6 months old. After her fully formula- fed infant reaches 6 months or age, the mother is no longer WIC-eligible.

Age of breastfed infant at first day of the month BF Within Range (standard formulas) BF Out of Range (standard formulas) 0 – 3 months 1 to 4 cans 5 to 9 cans 4 – 5 months 1 to 5 cans 6 to 10 cans 6 – 12 months 1 to 4 cans 5 to 7 cans

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services

Revised: 04/01/2025

Page 2 of 6

Infants 11 month of age until their first birthday Issue an infant food package to all infants, including those between 11 and 12 months of age. If the recertification occurs during the month the child turns one year of age, recertify using the Infant Nutrition Interview, assign infant nutrition risk factors, and issue an infant food package for the full month. Issue a child (toddler) food package at the beginning of the month when the child has already turned one year of age.

Medical Indication for Formula Certain medical indications may pose a temporary or long term problem for breastfeeding and require supplementation of formula or banked human milk (although banked human milk is not a WIC-eligible food, as defined by 7 CFR 246.10). Staff must work with mothers to determine the amount of formula that the food package shall contain and the length of time the doctor recommended the supplement, particularly if the need is for a standard formula and there is no prescription. If the mother does not know, staff will recommend she contact her infant’s health care provider.  Maternal medical indications:  Breast anatomical challenges (e.g., tubular breasts or marked breast asymmetry, inverted nipples for which shields and pumping alone will not suffice).  Breast surgery (e.g., reduction, augmentation, abscesses, cancer).  Endocrine abnormality (e.g., diabetes, pituitary insufficiency – noted as a lack of noticeable breast changes during pregnancy, failure of lactogenesis stage 2 – milk did not noticeably come in) .  Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Mothers with PCOS are at greater risk for insufficient milk supply, however many mothers with PCOS do not experience breastfeeding challenges and produce ample milk.  Perinatal complications (e.g., hypertension, hemorrhage, retained placental fragments).  Contraindicated medication.  Infant medical indications:  Premature (<37 weeks/0 days gestation) or very low birth weight.  Excessive weight loss (not regained birth weight by 14 days of age or loss of more than 10% of birth weight).  Acute dehydration not responsive to routine breastfeeding.  Breastfeeding jaundice.  Hypoglycemia.  Inborn errors of metabolism (e.g., PKU).  Special formula needed.  Not feeding well at discharge and sent home pumping with a formula supplement (should be followed by a physician within 24-72 hours after discharge).

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services

Revised: 04/01/2025

Page 3 of 6

No Medical Indication for Formula If there is no medical indication, promote any amount of breastfeeding, ask open-ended questions to understand the reason for the formula request, affirm the parent’s breastfeeding success so far (promote any amount of breastfeeding), and provide information and troubleshoot with the mother. Infant formula should only be provided to infants after evaluation and counseling by the High Risk Counselor, WLS, or DBE.

If, after counseling and education, the mother chooses to receive formula, tailor the food package to best meet, but not exceed, the nutritional needs of the infant. First, determine if the infant is already receiving formula, then change the infant’s breastfeeding description to “part BF” and provide only the minimum amount of formula needed.

Work with the mother to create food packages that best support her breastfeeding plan, explaining that smaller formula packages may enable her to receive more food for herself with a food package for partially breastfeeding women.

Infant Formulas Categories Infant formulas are classified into three categories:

1. Primary Contract Brand Infant Formula: Any (standard) infant formula manufactured by the company with whom Colorado WIC has a formula rebate contract. (See MPSF: WC-00-25-P). A prescription is not required for WIC to issue primary contract brand infant formula. a. All infants enrolled on the Colorado WIC Program receiving a standard infant formula should receive one of five primary contract brand infant formulas: Enfamil Infant, Enfamil ProSobee, Enfamil Gentlease, Enfamil Reguline or Enfamil AR. Mead Johnson Nutritionals contracts with Colorado WIC to provide rebate dollars for each container of Enfamil Infant, Enfamil ProSobee, Enfamil Gentlease, Enfamil Reguline or Enfamil AR issued to WIC participants. Rebate money is used to support additional caseload.

Contract for Infant Formula Rebate: Federal regulations require that state WIC Programs contract with a single infant formula manufacturer. Additionally, federal regulations require the use of Primary Contract Brand Infant Formulas, except when contraindicated by a specific medical condition. The Colorado WIC Program contracts with Mead Johnson Nutritionals to be the provider of standard milk and soy-based formulas. These formulas contain at least 10 mg iron per liter and 20 kilocalories per fluid ounce. Rebates for the contract formulas, which are used to enroll more children and women in WIC, support a significant percentage of the Colorado WIC caseload. There are no exceptions for the provision of standard formulas made by other manufacturers.

Colorado WIC receives rebate for the following formulas:  Enfamil Infant - A milk-based formula.  Enfamil ProSobee – A soy-based formula.  Enfamil Gentlease - A reduced-lactose milk-based formula that has partially hydrolyzed protein.  Enfamil Reguline – A milk-based formula with added prebiotics.  Enfamil AR – A milk-based formula with added rice starch.

2. Non-Contract Brand Infant Formula: Any infant formula or exempt infant formula that is not a contract formula. (See MPSF:WC-00-25-P)

3. Exempt Infant Formula. Any infant formula designed for infants with special medical conditions who require a modified infant formula. (See FDC Act 21 U.S.C. 350a). Exempt infant formulas are those that are represented and labeled for use by an infant who has an inborn error of metabolism, a low birth weight or who otherwise has an unusual medical or dietary problem. They are often used with infants who have medical problems that affect their nutritional needs and/or their ability to digest regular infant formulas. It is very important that a physician regularly reevaluate the need and acceptance by an infant receiving an exempt infant formula.

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services

Revised: 04/01/2025

Page 4 of 6

Issuance of an exempt infant formula is only permitted with a properly completed Colorado WIC Program’s Physician Authorization Form or a physician’s prescription and High Risk Counselor approval of prescription prior to issuance. It is important that a physician regularly reevaluates the appropriateness of the type and amount of the formula or nutritional prescribed. For more information, see Prescription Required Formulas and Nutritionals policy in Section 2, Nutrition Services.

Formulas to Accommodate Religious Beliefs: In the event that one of Colorado WIC’s contract formulas does not meet a participant’s religious requirements, such as need for a kosher formula, a non-contract formula can be issued without a physician’s authorization. Documentation of the issuance of a non-contract formula to accommodate religious eating patterns must be included in the participant’s record.

Issuance of Ready-To-Feed Federal and State regulations require that infant formulas be issued in concentrated liquid or powder physical forms. Ready-to-feed (RTF) WIC formulas may be authorized when the CWA determines and documents that:  The family’s water supply is contaminated and / or is unsafe for consumption.  The caregiver has difficulty correctly diluting concentrate or powder formula.  For a medically fragile infant (i.e. premature).  The formula only comes in ready-to-feed form.

Banked Human Milk Banked human milk is not a WIC-eligible supplemental food and WIC federal funds cannot be used for the purposes of collecting, storing, purchasing, or disseminating banked human milk.

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services

Revised: 04/01/2025
