body:
Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services Revised: 01/01/2025 Page 1 of 2

Nutrition Assessment

Policy: Staff must conduct a thorough nutritional assessment, which includes completing a Nutrition Interview. A nutrition interview must be completed at certification, recertification and mid-certification appointments. All questions within the Nutrition Interview must be asked and documented. The exceptions to this include: • The anthropometrics fields for the the biological mother and father. • Local agencies that need to suspend referrals to the Breastfeeding Peer Counseling (BFPC) program for caseload management purposes may skip the BFPC support question.

Many questions lead to assignment of risk factors. Breastfeeding information within the interview may be updated as needed at follow-up appointments.

Note: Some questions in the Nutrition Interview are in bold font, this indicates questions used for data surveillance.

Regulation: CRF 246.4(a)(19)

Procedure/Additional Guidance: A thorough WIC nutrition assessment evaluates the following areas:  Growth  Iron/Lead Screening  Health/Medical  Nutrition Practices  Lifestyle  Personal Factors

Growth: Growth is assessed by taking anthropometric measures on a regular basis and tracking growth patterns. Measures used to assess growth include: stature/weight, BMI, and prenatal weight gain. Growth is an important indicator of nutritional status. For example, poor growth may reflect inadequate nutritional intake or signal an underlying medical problem. Overweight can be associated with current or future health problems in both children and adults. Deviations from normal growth should be referred for follow up since early identification and intervention can prevent more serious health outcomes.

Iron/Lead Screening: Iron levels are measured regularly by performing either a hemoglobin or hematocrit test. The purpose of iron screening is to identify and prevent anemia (low iron in the blood). Lead levels for children are recorded from screenings done outside of WIC. Elevated blood lead levels can adversely affect behavior, development, and IQ. If a child has not had a lead testing, they must be referred to programs where they can obtain such a test.

Health/Medical: Health and Medical history and current conditions are assessed using the Nutrition Interview. Examples of medical conditions that have nutrition implications are: diseases (such as PKU, diabetes, high blood pressure), food allergies, and physical and mental disabilities. Additionally, medications can affect appetite. High-risk medical conditions require a follow up appointment with the high risk counselor at each certification period within 30 days of high risk identification.

Nutrition Practices: The WIC nutrition practices assessment is conducted through dialogue with the client about breastfeeding, if applicable, the foods they usually eat and their regular eating patterns. Using a discussion format, the WIC educator begins the interview with open-ended question asking the client to describe their typical eating and drinking habits. The educator evaluates the client’s response against professionally recognized guidelines (e.g. Dietary Guidelines for Americans, My Plate Food Guide, and American Academy of Pediatrics) and the following criteria that are associated with a healthy diet:  A variety of foods derived from different food groups  Few processed foods in the diet  Majority of foods consumed are nutrient dense (they contain a lot of vitamins and minerals)  The amount of food eaten is appropriate

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services Revised: 01/01/2025 Page 2 of 2  Good eating habits (this includes having family meals, eating at set times rather than grazing, children not drinking from the bottle, etc.)

Then, based on the client’s responses, the WIC staff person asks further questions to obtain additional information and/or clarify what has been said.

Breastfeeding complications and the breastfeeding description are included on the Infant Nutrition Interview under Nutrition Practices. The following table identifies an infant or child’s breastfeeding status:

Description Definition Exclusively Breastfeeding Has been fed only human milk, vitamins, minerals, and/or medications. (This is equivalent to the CDC definition of exclusive) Primarily Exclusive/ No Formula Package

Has been fed something other than human milk, vitamins, minerals and/or medications on rare occasion or one time feeding of infant formula, human milk fortifier, cow’s milk, juice, sugar water, rehydration solution, water, baby food, or anything else. This identifies an infant whose exclusive breastfeeding is interrupted because of special circumstances (e.g., acute illness, hospitalization, caregiver misinformation) is fed. Primarily Exclusive/ Complementary Foods

Has been fed any complementary foods (e.g. cereal, baby food, table foods) in addition to only being fed human milk, vitamins, minerals and/or medications. These foods are provided on a routine or ongoing basis regardless of the amount. Partially Breastfeeding Breastfeeding and receiving formula (WIC or non WIC supplied formula). May also be fed complementary foods. Breastfeeding Child Greater than or equal to 12 months and continuing breastfeeding. No Longer Breastfeeding Was breastfeeding at some point in time but has now discontinued. Never Breastfed Was never breastfed.

Lifestyle: Assessment of lifestyle involves finding out about physical activity (including the types and amounts of physical activity they get) and substance use (such as abuse or exposure to alcohol, drugs, cigarettes or second hand smoke).

Immunizations: Immunization information is captured during the infant and child interview for DTaP shot records only.

Oral Health: Oral health information is captured during the infant and child interview to obtain information regarding dental and other oral health concerns.

Breastfeeding Support: For all breastfeeding women, breastfeeding support is included as part of the assessment during the nutrition interview. Breastfeeding complications and assignment of the BFPC are captured on this panel.

Social Environment: Social Environment includes: culture, family structure, education, living and work situations, abuse/neglect, family planning and primary caregiver with limited ability to make appropriate feeding decisions. Understanding social environment enables WIC staff to provide client centered care and individualized referrals and counseling.

body:
Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services Revised: 10/01/2023

Page 1 of 3

Nutrition Education

Policy: Local agencies shall offer nutrition education at no cost to all WIC participants, parents, or caregivers according to federal regulations and state guidelines Agencies have the option to enter into an agreement with another agency to offer participant nutrition education.

Nutrition education may be provided through individual or group sessions. During each six-month certification period, at least two nutrition education contacts must be made available. When participants are certified for longer than six months, nutrition contacts shall be made available at a quarterly rate.

Nutrition education shall be participant-centered and include behavior change counseling. Goals must be set and followed-up on at subsequent appointments.

Note: A chart review does not count as a nutrition education contact for low or high risk participants.

Regulation: [246.11(b)]: 246.11(d)

Procedure/Additional Guidance: WIC provides nutrition education along with supplemental foods to guide participants toward a healthier lifestyle and to help them make changes to improve their dietary intake. Using a participant-centered approach helps to enhance the effectiveness of these activities.

Type of Nutrition Education Contacts In-Person Education: An in-person visit with the participant is provided either individually or in a group, and includes participant-centered nutrition education. A participant-centered nutrition education approach should address participant needs (NRFs), participant concerns, and/or relevant anticipatory guidance topics. Ideally, only 1-2 topics are addressed during a single visit. Topics not discussed during the appointment can be entered into the participant’s Plan to be addressed at a future visit.

Remote Education: Remote nutrition education options include:  Phone: As with in person education, provide participant-centered education. All required components of a WIC visit must be performed per policy, including nutrition education, goal setting, and documentation. During the end of the phone contact, food benefits will be issued remotely, and a subsequent visit scheduled.  Wichealth.org: An internet-based, online nutrition education website available in English and Spanish. Verification that the endorser completed a wichealth.org nutrition education lesson automatically uploads into the household’s Nutrition Education panel in Compass. Completion of a corresponding Care Plan is not required. The goal set at the prior in-person or phone appointment may be followed-up on at the nutrition education contact. Upon completion of an online lesson and during the month the participant’s food benefits expire; staff will verify the lesson completion, contact the participant, and issue food benefits remotely. Program and nutrition-related assistance and follow up must be available to address questions and to provide feedback to endorsers. Note: This education contact option is only for low-risk participants.  Interactive Video Call: Technology that allows video conference calls. As with in person education, provide participant-centered education. All required components of a WIC visit must be performed per policy, including nutrition education, goal setting, and documentation. During the end of the video call contact, food benefits will be issued remotely, and a subsequent visit scheduled. The local agency will provide for installation and maintenance of the equipment necessary for the video call contact. Interactive video calls should occur in an environment that promotes effective communication between the WIC staff and the participant and ensures that both are actively involved in the interaction. The confidentiality of participant information must be protected.

Providing Participant-Centered/Behavior Change Counseling

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services Revised: 10/01/2023

Page 2 of 3

The education part of the visit should flow naturally from the assessment because it ties in with the participant‘s questions and concerns. However, sometimes no clear direction emerges and in this case, the WIC staff person works with the participant to develop an agenda for topics to discuss. Ways to do this are:  Ask the participant about any nutrition questions or concerns they would like to discuss. Nutrition information provided during the visit should match the participant’s needs and interests.  Suggest topics based on information gathered during the assessment.  Suggest topics that provide anticipatory guidance.

Tips for discussing nutrition information with participants:  Use a conversational format.  Find out what the participant already knows about a topic and fill in the gaps.  Affirm the things that are going well.  Be non-judgmental.  Personalize education so the participant understands how making changes can improve their health and well- being.

Readiness to Change Counseling While sharing nutrition information, WIC staff should assess the participant’s interest in applying the information to their life by making behavior changes. Sometimes participants are ready to change. Sometimes they are not. Or they might be anywhere between. It is important to get a sense for how ready to change a participant is in order to tailor counseling to meet them where they are. Applying readiness to change counseling is useful for providing ideas for ways to approach participants who are in different stages of readiness to change. The chart below describes readiness to change and the recommended counseling strategy associated with it. Readiness to Change Counseling

Level of Readiness to Change Counseling Strategy

Not Ready or thinking about changing Raise awareness. Be prepared not to push for change. This is likely to cause more resistance.

Uncertain about making a change Explore pros/cons of change, concerns/fears

Ready to change Have the participant talk about the reasons for, importance of, or their plans for change.

Goal Setting Goal setting is an important component of behavior change counseling because it encourages the participant to put into action something discussed during the appointment. The goals set with participants will differ depending on their readiness to change. For participants not ready to change, appropriate goals are ones that help to raise awareness or encourage the participant to think through the pros and cons of change. Examples of goals that are appropriate for no or low readiness to change are to simply read over educational material, to talk to a partner, or to think about what it would look like to make a specific change. These goals may not seem very ambitious; however, they are realistic and consistent with the participant’s motivation and readiness to change. As the participant becomes more committed to making a change, appropriate goals will be ones that are more action oriented. For example, the goal may be to have the participant take small steps toward making the behavior change.

When setting goals with participants it is important to remember these principles:  Goal setting should be done interactively with the participant. WIC staff’s role is to suggest ideas for goals that might be appropriate for the participant’s readiness to change. It is the participant’s role to make the decision about what they are able and willing to do.  Goals should be specific. A clearly stated goal is easier to follow.  Write down the goal (perhaps on a handout) as a reminder after they leave the appointment.

Documentation - Document the goal in the Participant Care Plan. The goal should be described clearly, so that WIC staff can easily follow up on the goal with the participant at the next appointment.

Follow up - Since behavior change is a process, it is important to follow up at the next visit by asking the participant about their progress in achieving their goal. Offer praise for any efforts they have made and provide support as appropriate. It may be necessary to adjust the goal to make it more doable.

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services Revised: 10/01/2023

Page 3 of 3

Following up on goals helps to increase the participant’s accountability, provides opportunities for support and problem solving, and demonstrates to the participant that WIC cares about helping them make changes. Document follow up discussion(s) about goals in either the Subjective or Assessment section of the Participant Care Plan.

Nutrition Educational Materials: WIC’s nutrition educational materials help reinforce educational messages. Certain materials are available to order in print and all materials are available electronically to share via email or text.

Missed Nutrition Education Appointments and Non-Denial of WIC Benefits Although local agencies are required to make reasonable efforts to provide nutrition education to each participant, individuals cannot be denied supplemental foods for failure to attend an educational activity or for lack of willingness, readiness, or ability to participate in the activity.

When a participant does not attend or participate in a scheduled nutrition education contact, document why this occurred in the Participant Care Plan.

When a participant misses a scheduled appointment, offer the nutrition education contact the next time you make contact with the participant.

body:
Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services Revised: 01/01/2025

Page 1 of 5 Screening (Substance Abuse, HIV/AIDs, Lead and Immunizations) and Referrals

Policy: Local WIC Programs should establish referral systems and provide appropriate health and social services referrals to participants.

Local WIC Programs are responsible for contacting referrals received through online referral systems or other methods within 10 days from the date of submission.

Regulation: Colorado WIC Policy, CFR 246.4 (a)(8) and (9) 246.7 (a) and (n), CFR 246.11 (a)(3) and (b)(1), CFR 246.14 (c)(1) and (9), USDA Memo 94-28

Procedures/Additional Guidance:

Referrals to WIC The Colorado PEAK online application allows a person using PEAK to select WIC as a program they wish to be contacted by. The PEAK system creates live reports, by county, of those interested individuals’ contact information. Designated local WIC agency staff manage referrals via a secure database.

The WIC Statewide Referral Form is an electronic form community partners and the public can use to submit requests for WIC to contact potentially-eligible WIC participants. Designated local WIC agency staff manage referrals via a secure database.

Development of Referral Systems The establishment of a local agency referral network consists of two components: identification of community resources and education of WIC staff on community resources.  A local referral network includes programs housed within the same agency as the WIC Program (intra- agency), as well as other community organizations (inter agency). The number of community agencies within the WIC Program service area will determine the size of the referral network.  To ensure participants are appropriately directed to other community services, it is necessary to inform all WIC staff about the organizations within the referral network. WIC staff should understand the purpose/function and eligibility criteria for each agency/organization in the network. o Several mechanisms could be used to inform the WIC staff members. Agency representatives can be invited to provide a short presentation at WIC staff meetings. Pamphlets from the various community organizations could be made available to the WIC staff. Maintaining a "community resource" notebook with these pamphlets would provide the staff with easy access.

Referrals can be informal (informing the client about the SNAP Program) or formal (sending a standardized referral form). This will depend on the reason for the referral. If the referral includes client information or requires local staff to contact the local program or organization on behalf of the family, the participant or endorser’s signature of consent must be obtained. If the endorser has granted permission to release information to the physician based on their answer provided in the Nutrition Interview, client information may be released to the physician. Referrals may be printed and given to the participant upon request.

Making Referrals Agencies have the option to provide either an informal or formal referral. Methods for each type of referral are described as follows:  Informal Referral: A referral can be accomplished simply by providing all adult participants and caretakers of participating infants and children with the list of available resources.  Formal Referral: A local agency may opt to develop a more formal referral system wherein a staff member initiates contact with a resource (e.g. substance abuse counseling or treatment agency) on behalf of an interested participant. Please note: Confidentiality rules must be followed.

It is recommended that all clients be directed informally to: • The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP)

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services Revised: 01/01/2025

Page 2 of 5 • Medicaid (Health First Colorado) • Child Health Plan Plus (CHP+) • Temporary Assistance to Needy Families (TANF) Programs, • Colorado PEAK at https://coloradopeak.secure.force.com (an on-line service for Coloradans to check for potential food and cash assistance programs, apply for Medicaid and Child Health Plan Plus programs, WIC, SNAP, TANF and Aging and Adult Services Financial programs and manage benefits on-line)

Staff should provide the addresses, web address and/or telephone numbers for these referral resources. The local WIC Program can obtain this information from the Social Services Agency.

Documenting Referrals All referrals by local WIC staff persons must be entered on the Referrals - Participant panel in the Compass system or noted in the participant’s Care Plan. All written information given to participants on assistance programs must be recorded.

Referral Follow-Up To ensure that quality nutritional care is provided to WIC clients, follow up should be provided on all referrals.

Substance Abuse Information and Referral The Colorado WIC Program screens for drug, alcohol, and tobacco use to determine nutrition/medical criterion through the use of questions asked on the Nutrition Interview. WIC staff must provide information on the dangers of drugs and other harmful substances and referrals to pregnant, postpartum, and breastfeeding women and to the parents and caretakers of WIC infants and children. Participants who indicate that they or their child are exposed to secondhand tobacco smoke must also be warned of the dangers to themselves and/or their children. Information must be provided in verbal form. Visuals, written communication and online resources may supplement the information provided verbally. Staff members are not expected to diagnose drug and other substance abuse or to provide in-depth counseling. Rather, they are to provide information on the dangers of substance abuse and secondhand smoke in the course of routine activities.

Federal Drug and Other Harmful Substance Abuse Information and Referral regulations specify the following requirements for all local WIC Programs:  Participants with suspected drug or other harmful substance abuse problems must be referred to an appropriate counseling, treatment or education program where services are locally available.  Each local agency must maintain and make available for distribution a list of local resources for substance abuse counseling and treatment. o (e.g., Alcoholics Anonymous, Narcotics Anonymous, Cocaine Anonymous, Al-Anon Family Groups, Adult Children of Alcoholics, Women for Sobriety), drug and alcohol treatment programs as well as local smoking cessation programs sponsored by organizations such as the American Lung Association and American Cancer Society. In communities where resources are limited, the public health nurse or the participant's physician should be considered as a possible resource.  Local agencies are required to coordinate with local alcohol and drug abuse treatment services.

HIV/AIDS Information and Referral The Colorado WIC Program can play an important role in preventing the transmission of HIV/AIDS in the perinatal population. The following guidelines define the policy for the WIC Program regarding issues related to HIV/AIDS and WIC participants:  Encourage comprehensive health care for all WIC participants.  Advise all pregnant, postpartum, and breastfeeding women to know their HIV status and receive early diagnosis through routine, voluntary testing, and counseling.  Provide appropriate referrals to participants for testing, counseling, and medical treatments as needed.  Strongly encourage and support breastfeeding as the healthiest way to feed infants.  Inform all participants that HIV-positive mothers should not breastfeed, and that HIV is more easily transmitted through breast milk during the period immediately following the onset of infection.

o The Colorado WIC Program concurs with the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment and United States Department of Agriculture to support the recommendations of the American

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services Revised: 01/01/2025

Page 3 of 5 Academy of Pediatrics and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention that women in the United States should not breastfeed if they are HIV positive or have AIDS.

Blood Lead Screening Information & Referral To implement the provision in Public Law 106-387, included in the WIC Appropriations Act FY2001, local WIC Programs are required to:  Ask if the child has had a blood lead screening test starting at 12 months of age.  If the child has not had a test, they must be referred (at each certification/midcert/recertification) to programs where they can obtain such a test.  Document lead screening referrals in the Nutrition Education Panel by selecting "Referred for Lead Screening" under child standard counseling.  Once a lead test has been performed and documented, screening and referral is no longer required.

The blood screen within the Assessment panel is where staff record if a child has received a blood lead screening test. In Colorado, lead testing is covered by Medicaid and the Child Health Plan Plus (CHP+). Additionally, most private insurance providers will cover the cost of the testing when the test is ordered by a physician. Some local health departments may also provide lead testing. Public Law 106-387 does not allow WIC funds to be used to conduct blood lead screening tests. A hematological test for anemia, such as a hemoglobin or hematocrit, is the only laboratory test required to determine a person’s eligibility for WIC. It is therefore, the only cost that may be charged to WIC.

Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA) Certification Number: Clinical laboratories are registered under the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA) federal regulation to ensure quality laboratory testing. All labs that perform testing on human specimens for diagnosis, treatment or health assessment in the United States must hold the appropriate CLIA certificate. The CLIA regulations set standards for personnel, records, quality control and quality assurance.  Each WIC local agency must operate under a CLIA Certificate. This CLIA Certificate is typically held by the Health Department, not by the WIC Program. Each WIC clinic needs to be listed on the CLIA Certificate, however if a local agency does not know their CLIA Certificate number (typically starts with “06D”), the WIC director may ask the Public Health director, lab manager or nurse manager in their agency. If an agency is unsure of their CLIA number, contact: Jeff Groff Program Manager EBAT and Laboratory Certification P 303.692.3681 | F 303.344.9965 8100 Lowry Blvd, Denver, CO 80230 jeff.groff@state.co.us

Immunization Screening, Information, and Referral Low-income children are less likely to be immunized than their higher-income counterparts, placing them at high risk for potentially serious diseases, such as diphtheria, pertussis, poliomyelitis, measles, mumps, and rubella. WIC staff members play a significant role in helping to improve the immunization rates for low-income infants and children by assessing immunization records, educating participants on the importance of immunizations and by making referrals as necessary to bring immunizations up-to-date.

Local WIC agencies are required to:  Ask caregivers of infants and children under 25 months of age to bring immunization records to all certification/recertification and mid-certification visits. Note: If the record is available in the Colorado Immunization Information System (CIIS), agencies with access to CIIS may access electronic records in lieu of obtaining the immunization information from the caregiver.  Assess immunization records for infants and children less than 25 months of age for recommended DTaP shots.  1st DTaP is at 2 months of age  2nd DTaP is at 4 months of age  3rd DTaP is at 6 months of age  4th DTaP is between 15 and 18 months of age

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 2: Nutrition Services Revised: 01/01/2025

Page 4 of 5  Provide information on the immunization schedule and refer caregivers to obtain immunizations if the infant or child’s immunizations are not up-to-date or the immunization record is not available.  Once a child has received their 4 DTaP immunizations, staff no longer need to ask about the child's immunization status. Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 3: MIS Revison Date: 10/01/2018

Page 1 of 1

Issue Resolution at the State WIC Help Desk

Policy: Report all suspected Compass application issues and data integrity issues to the State WIC Compass Help Desk.

Regulation: Colorado WIC Policy

Procedure/Additional Guidance: Computer, Network and Internet Issues Compass is a web-based system that relies on local area networks and Internet connectivity that is created and maintained by county IT departments. Therefore, some problems must be resolved by the county or local agency IT staff.

When a local agency WIC user encounters a network, computer equipment malfunction, computer login or Internet problem, please contact the local agency IT unit as the first level of support. The local IT unit should be able to solve most reported problems. If the local agency IT determines that additional state support is required to resolve an issue, have a technical person contact the State WIC Compass help desk for level II support.

Compass Application Issues The WIC Compass Help Desk will investigate the system concern and if they determine that an application error might exist, the Help Desk will create a ticket and the issue will then be reviewed and resolved. The fix will be included in a future release of a new Compass version. If the State WIC Compass Help Desk determines that the application is working correctly, they will provide the local agency or staff person with an explanation and possible written system documentation on the application behavior. As a final step, the State WIC Compass Help Desk may escalate the ticket to the local agency assigned Nutrition Consultant or Compass Training Coordinator if it appears that the problem is a matter of training or policy. The State WIC Help Desk may send it to Level 2 Technical Support if the problem appears to be of a more complex technical nature.

Data Issues The Help Desk will investigate the concern and if they determine that a data integrity issue may exist, they will immediately escalate the issue to the State Database Administrator for further investigation and resolution.

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 3: MIS Revised: 01/01/2022

Page 1 of 1

WIC Compass User Access

Policy: Local WIC Agency Directors must complete necessary forms to ensure that Compass user access is granted to Compass users who actively work at a specific WIC clinic. The Compass Access Request Form must be completed and submitted each time a new staff person is hired, when their position responsibilities change and when their WIC employment ends.

Regulation: Colorado WIC Policy

Procedure/Additional Guidance: Compass Application and Data Security The Compass system requires a user to log into the system using credentials created by the WIC Compass Care Team. The Compass Access Request Form includes the data security, use, and confidentiality agreement that each employee must read and sign. Signatures from the WIC supervisor and WIC employee are required and the printed copy can be faxed or scanned & emailed to the WIC Compass Care Team

Staff can change their passwords after a successful log on using the provided User ID and Password. User IDs and passwords are not to be shared with others. Every 120 days, Compass prompts the user that the old password is about to expire and a new password must be entered. Passwords must be strong to be secure. Strong passwords are at least 8 characters in length, have a mixed case (some capitals and some lowercase letters), have at least one number, and have a special character.

For data security purpose and to ensure that only active user’s have access to the Compass sytem, the Colorado WIC State Office will deactivate any user who has not been active in Compass for 8 weeks. Staff that are inactive for 8 weeks due to situations such as medical leave, can be reactivated by submitting a ticket in Elementool.

Colorado WIC Program Policies & Procedures Section 4: Organization and Management Revised: 07/01/2026

Page 1 of 4

Data Use Policy: Use of Program Participant and Applicant Data

Policy: WIC staff, state and local, direct all requests for the disclosure of individual-level, identifying WIC participant information (i.e., any non-aggregated data) to the Data Manager at the Colorado WIC State Office. The following policy is used to assess the ability to fulfill data requests.

Regulation: Federal:7 CFR 246.26, 7 CFR 246.7(i)(11), 7 CFR 246.3(h)(3) State: § 24-74-102(1), C.R.S. and § 24-74-103 CRS

Procedure/Additional Guidance: This data use policy clarifies when and how Colorado WIC State Program participant data will be shared with state, local, and external entities while protecting participant confidentiality.

Aggregated Data Aggregated data arise from processing individual records into summary form in order to track information across populations, organizations, time and other variables of interest. State and local Colorado WIC Program staff may access aggregated data via WIC Data Central (WDC) and Compass reports. Requests for additional aggregated data not available on WDC or within Compass reports shall be directed to the Data Manager.

Maintaining Statistical Stability Aggregated WIC data sometimes describe rare events and/or small populations, which may compromise statistical stability. Therefore, when possible, aggregated data produced by the Data Manager shall include a description of the variability of the data (i.e., confidence intervals, relative standard error). Additionally, the Data Manager will recommend the requester interpret any counts of less than 30 with caution given the small sample size.

Maintaining Confidentiality When data use occurs outside of state and local Colorado WIC Program staff, rare events and small populations may also endanger participant confidentiality. Counts of 20 or less will be censored when producing tables that will be viewed outside of state or local WIC staff to maintain confidentiality. The Data Manager also uses caution when sharing aggregate data with populations of less than 500, and producing multiple tables from the same dataset. Should there be concern about a possible breach of confidentiality when sharing outside of state and local WIC staff, the Data Manager will take steps to limit this risk through strategies such as: combining alike groups, producing a courser analysis, and omitting tables unlikely to contain information that would inform public health efforts.

Personally Identifying Information (PII) Per Federal regulations (§246.26), PII includes any information that individually identifies an applicant, participant, and/or family member(s) that was obtained or created during the course of an individual(s) WIC referral, application, or program participation. This includes but is not limited to: name; WIC participant number; contact information (may include address, phone, email); health data; the fact that a person was referred, applied, and/or participated in WIC; date of birth; health insurance number; source of income; status as a recipient of public assistance; race; ethnicity; gender identity; physical, intellectual and/or developmental disability.

In accordance with Federal regulation §246.7(i)(11), WIC applicants and participants acknowledge in the Participant Rights & Responsibilities form through the following language that their PII may be shared for these allowed purposes: ● “WIC respects my privacy. Information I give is used to verify if I qualify and to provide me with services. My information may be shared only with programs directly connected with WIC and for reports and audits as approved by the Colorado WIC Data Use Policy. Any other sharing of information must be approved by me with a signed or verbal consent.” ● “WIC staff are mandatory reporters. They are required to report suspected child abuse or neglect.”

Colorado WIC Program Policies & Procedures Section 4: Organization and Management Revised: 07/01/2026

Page 2 of 4

The local Colorado WIC agency must permit applicants and participants to refuse to sign/acknowledge the Rights & Responsibilities statement but must also notify the applicants and participants that signing/acknowledging the form is a condition of program eligibility and participation. These forms must be signed/acknowledged only after the certification is complete.

A verbal acknowledgment is allowed instead of a signature for those participants who are participating in a remote appointment.

Prior to PII disclosure for the allowed purposes listed below, the state WIC agency requires a completed data request process. If the request is approved, a data use agreement is created to include: a) Specific PII to be shared, why PII is critically necessary, the intended purpose of PII, time frame of PII use, specific individuals with access to PII, plan for safekeeping and timely destruction of PII, and assurance that the partner will not use the information for any other purpose or disclose the information to a third party. b) Approval of the Colorado WIC director, the director of the CDPHE Office of Legal & Regulatory Compliance, and CDPHE Privacy Officer. c) Signature of the Executive Director of CDPHE. d) Amendment to the WIC State Plan in accordance with federal regulation §246.3(h)(3).

The Colorado State WIC Program provides only the PII reasonably necessary to accomplish the approved purpose(s). The initiation of a data request does not compel the Colorado WIC Program to provide PII to the requestor. The Colorado State WIC office will make every attempt to use aggregated data in lieu of disclosing PII in meeting the needs of a requestor. If a request cannot use aggregated data and does not present a clear benefit to applicants/participants or the Colorado State WIC program as a whole, the request will be denied.

If the data requested requires matching or may involve research, Colorado State WIC follows the Prevention Services Division procedure related to these types of requests.

In alignment with USDA Food and Nutrition Service (FNS) Instruction 800-1, State WIC does not allow the use of universal consents which give an agency unlimited authority to release applicant or participant information, or to take the place of sharing agreements with health and welfare organizations detailed in the regulations. Such open- ended release forms could result in inappropriate sharing of information and reduce the protection of applicant/participant PII.

Disclosure to WIC staff for WIC Purposes State WIC provides access to PII to state and local WIC staff who administer WIC programming through the data management information system, Compass. Only authorized users are allowed access to this information; no non-WIC staff can be authorized for this access. Notification must be provided as to how the data may be used or shared.

Disclosure to Participant’s Healthcare Provider Participants may consent or deny consent to disclosure of personal information to their healthcare providers. This consent or denial of consent is recorded in Compass in the Nutrition Interview and a signature is captured when the participant signs the Colorado WIC Rights & Responsibilities document. The Colorado WIC Rights & Responsibilities states, “I have been asked about disclosing my confidential healthcare information with my provider. That information can be found in the Nutrition Interview.” Prior to documenting a participant’s preference (Yes or No) for disclosing information to their healthcare provider, the participant must be notified that their answer (consent or denial) is not a condition of their eligibility, and the possible reasons why information may be shared with their provider.

Any information shared with the healthcare provider should be minimum necessary. Minimum necessary means only the relevant information needed to accomplish the task can be shared.

Limited Disclosure to Non-WIC Partners for Approved Purposes Limited disclosure is a one-time release of information and does not include back and forth data sharing. The approved purposes for limited disclosure are listed below.

Colorado WIC Program Policies & Procedures Section 4: Organization and Management Revised: 07/01/2026

Page 3 of 4

● Non-WIC partners may only use PII with individual, documented participant consent to follow up on referrals and provide additional services to participants and their families. ● Non-WIC partners may use PII under a data use agreement to support evidence-based or promising practices that increase WIC enrollment and/or retention.

Note: Local WIC MOUs with partners that include sharing of WIC data are not allowed.

Disclosure Related to Subpoenas Per Federal regulation (§246.26), local WIC agencies receiving subpoenas shall immediately do the following; 1) Immediately notify the Colorado WIC Program State Office; 2) Notify local legal counsel, however local legal counsel cannot authorize release of PII. CDPHE legal counsel determines this. 3) If the requested information is PII, CDPHE legal will attempt to quash the subpoena unless CDPHE legal counsel determines that disclosing the PII is in the best interest of the Colorado State WIC Program. a) The decision to disclose PII without attempting to quash a subpoena should be made rarely and the Colorado State WIC Program should inform the receiving party that the requested information is confidential, provide only the specific information requested in the subpoena and no other information, and limit, to the greatest extent possible, public access to the disclosed PII. This may require a signed data sharing agreement at the discretion of the Colorado WIC Program Director and Data Manager.

Disclosure Related to Court Orders Local WIC agencies presented with a court order shall do the following: 1) Immediately notify the Colorado WIC Program State Office. The State Office will consult with CDPHE legal for direction.

Disclosure Related to Judicial Search Warrants A judicial search warrant is a court order signed by a judge/magistrate based on probable cause for criminal investigations, authorizing forced entry. In responding to a judicial search warrant for PII, the local Colorado WIC Program agency shall do the following: 1) Immediately notify the Colorado State WIC Program Director. 2) Immediately notify local legal counsel. 3) Comply with the judicial search warrant, but inform the individual(s) serving the judicial search warrant that the information being sought is confidential. 4) Seek to limit the disclosure by: a) Providing only the specific information requested in the judicial search warrant and no other information; and b) Limiting public access to the confidential information disclosed.

Disclosure to US Department of Agriculture (USDA)/FNS State and local WIC and contractors must cooperate in studies and evaluations conducted by or on behalf of the USDA, related to programs authorized under the Richard B. Russell National School Lunch Act and the Child Nutrition Act of 1966 (42 U.S.C. 1786).

Release of WIC Records to Endorser The Colorado State WIC Program releases applicant/participant records to the current initial and/or additional endorser(s) only for the period of time they personally are the endorser. The Colorado State WIC Program is only required to release information that was provided by the applicant/participant, except as required by federal, state or local law. The endorser(s) must show proof of identification (as defined by Colorado WIC Program proof of identity standards) to obtain the records and may only be provided with the portion of the record for which they were the endorser(s).

Colorado WIC Program Policies & Procedures Section 4: Organization and Management Revised: 07/01/2026

Page 4 of 4

Records Not Released Colorado WIC Program records shall not be released to the federal government or third parties, including the Department of Social Services (DSS), without written approval from the Colorado WIC Program or the endorser. Records of a child in foster care may only be released to DSS for that time while the child was in foster care. Requests for records from proxies, past or interim endorsers, relatives, or nonlegal guardians shall not be released. Requests for records for immigration or immigration administration purposes shall not be released. Records requests and releases shall be documented in each participant's care plan.

Direct questions or concerns about this policy to the Colorado WIC Program Director or the Data Manager.

Colorado WIC Program Policies & Procedures Section 4: Organization and Management Revised: 01.01.2021

Page 1 of 2

Data Use Policy: Process to Request Participant and Applicant Data

Policy: WIC staff, state and local, direct all requests for the disclosure of individual-level, identifying WIC participant information (i.e., any non-aggregated data) to the Data Manager at the Colorado WIC State Program Office.

Regulation: 7 CFR 246.26, 7 CFR 246.7(i)(11), 7 CFR 246.3(h)(3)

Procedure/Additional Guidance:

Introduction and Background State agencies administering the WIC program are responsible for the management and protection of confidential WIC applicant and participant information. The Colorado WIC State Program carries out these responsibilities according to state agency policies that ensure compliance with Federal regulations. The USDA grants state agencies the authority to determine with whom confidential WIC applicant and participant information will be shared and for what purposes within the limitations and allowances established in Federal regulation.

Colorado WIC Program policy requires that non-WIC partners may only use PII with participant consent for the following reasons: 1) to follow up on referrals and provide additional services to participants and their families. 2) under a data use agreement to support evidence-based or promising practices that increase WIC enrollment and/or retention. 3) reporting known or suspected child abuse or neglect.

The intent of this request process is to guide public partner organizations who desire use of confidential personal information for meaningful projects that benefit WIC applicants/participants or the Colorado WIC Program. Completion of this request will provide the Colorado WIC State Program Office sufficient information to assess whether the data use purpose meets Federal regulations and upholds program data use values. Expected time for review is within 10 business days. The Colorado WIC Program Director has the authority to approve or decline this request. If a request for data use is approved, additional information about data elements and timelines may be needed to create a data use agreement with all approved parties for approved uses.

In addition to compliance with Federal regulations, the Colorado WIC Program makes decisions regarding data use according to Program policies and values. The Colorado WIC State Program Office intends to support innovation proposed by state and local partners with these values in mind:

 The protection of confidential participant and applicant data is the highest level of priority for the Colorado WIC Program to build and maintain public trust that personal data is protected.  The Colorado WIC Program holds the interests, desires, and well-being of the public, WIC participants, and WIC applicants at the center of any data use decision. The Colorado WIC Program will ensure that any data use allowed within Federal regulations provides benefit to program participants, applicants and/or to the Colorado WIC Program as a whole.  Racial and ethnic equity will be preserved by ensuring that no data use agreements result in any type of harm to people or communities of color or any people or communities impacted by public charge.  The Colorado WIC Program will ensure that only the minimum necessary protected information is provided through data use agreements.  Robust protections of personal data by the recipient organization will be ensured by the Colorado WIC Program before approving data use agreements.  Data use requests will be balanced with capacity and resource constraints of the Colorado WIC Program, as the Program does not typically receive additional funding for these purposes.

Colorado WIC Program Policies & Procedures Section 4: Organization and Management Revised: 01.01.2021

Page 2 of 2

Request Process Please answer the following questions to request confidential personally-identifiable information (PII) from the Colorado WIC Program:

 What effort or intervention does your organization plan to execute using Colorado WIC Program data? In your response, please describe how your proposal meets at least one of these state requirements for use of PII with participant consent by non-WIC partners: ○ to follow up on referrals and provide additional services to participants and their families. ○ under a data use agreement to support evidence-based or promising practices that increase WIC enrollment and/or retention. ○ reporting known or suspected child abuse or neglect.

 What evidence demonstrates that this effort or intervention has a promising or proven impact for Colorado WIC Program participants?

 Has your organization conducted engagement work with Colorado WIC Program participants to understand their perspective about your effort or intervention? If yes, please answer the following: ○ In what ways has participant engagement informed your planned effort or intervention? ○ What has the engagement work revealed about participants’ perceived benefit of this proposal? ○ What has your community engagement revealed about participants' level of comfort for the Colorado WIC Program using their personal data for these purposes?

 If your organization hopes to streamline administrative procedures and minimize staff burden, have you engaged Colorado WIC Program (state or local) staff for their perspective about the proposal? If yes, what do they perceive as the benefit to their administrative roles?

 What interventions do you hope to do differently based on the availability of this data? How may this change if this request is denied?

 During or after your effort or intervention, what findings would you share with the Colorado WIC Program about the outcomes, impacts, and discoveries of your work that could benefit the future direction of the Program statewide?

 What specific additional value does PII data provide that cannot be met by available sources of aggregate data provided by the Colorado WIC Program?

 Data Security: ○ If this request is approved, who specifically will see and/or utilize Colorado WIC Program data? Please include names, titles, a description of their roles, the name of the entities for which they work, and a description of where they appear in an organizational chart (division, unit, and which positions they report to). ○ Where and how would data from the Colorado WIC Program be stored? ○ What is your planned destruction method for sensitive data? When and would the data from the Colorado WIC Program be destroyed? ○ How can the Colorado WIC Program audit the handling of the data to ensure proper use? ○ What safeguards do you have in place to ensure Colorado WIC Program data will not be used in any way that might harm the individuals represented in the data?

 What long term or future work is planned that relates to this work and the Colorado WIC Program data used for this immediate project?

 Have you gotten permission from your organization to enter into a data use agreement with the Colorado WIC Program, if needed? If so, who would sign the agreement for your organization or program (include name, title, contact information)?

 Please submit your data request electronically to the WIC Data Manager, cdphe_nsbdata@state.co.us.

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 4: Organization and Management Revised: 03/01/2026

Page 1 of 2

Homeless and Domestic Violence Shelters: Approval and Closure Process

Policy: The State or local agency shall attempt to establish to the extent practicable, that the homeless facility meets the following conditions with respect to resident WIC participants: ● The homeless facility does not accrue financial or in-kind benefit from a person's participation in the Program, e.g., by reducing its expenditures for food service because its residents are receiving WIC foods; ● Foods provided by the WIC Program are not included into a communal food service, but are available exclusively to the WIC participant for whom they were issued; ● The homeless facility places no constraints on the ability of the participant to partake of the supplemental foods, nutrition education and breastfeeding support available under the Program.

The local agency staff shall: ● Contact the homeless facility periodically to ensure continued compliance with these conditions; and ● Request the homeless facility to notify the State or local agency if it ceases to meet any of these conditions.

Regulation: 7 CFR 246.4, 7 CRF 246.7

Procedure/Additional Guidance: Homeless Facility: Any of the following facilities which provide meal service: a publicly supervised or privately operated shelter, including a welfare hotel or congregate shelter, designed to provide temporary living accommodations; a facility that provides a temporary residence for individuals intended to be institutionalized; and a public or private place not designed for, or ordinarily used as, a regular sleeping accommodation for human beings.

Homeless Individuals: A woman, infant or child who lacks a fixed and regular nighttime residence; or whose primary nighttime residence is a supervised publicly or privately operated shelter (including a welfare hotel, a congregate shelter, or a shelter for victims of domestic violence) designated to provide temporary living accommodation; an institution that provides a temporary residence for individuals intended to be institutionalized; a temporary accommodation of not more than 365 days in the residence of another individual; or a public or private place not designed for, or ordinarily used as, a regular sleeping accommodation for human beings.

Steps for Approving A Shelter The steps for approving a shelter are as follows: 1. Local agency forwards name and address of facility wishing to become a WIC-eligible homeless shelter to the State WIC Office. 2. State Office sends information and an Application for Approval of a Homeless Shelter (WIC #90) to the shelter. 3. Shelter returns the completed form to the State Office. 4. State Office reviews the form for ability and willingness to comply with required eligibility conditions. If the shelter meets criteria, they become provisionally authorized. 5. State Office sends Letter of Agreement signed by State staff with provisional authorization to the shelter. A copy is sent to the local WIC agency to inform staff of the need to visit the shelter. 6. A representative of the local WIC Program visits the shelter within 60 days to conduct an initial orientation visit. This visit will serve as an opportunity for the local WIC Program to become more familiar with the facility, review compliance with the Letter of Agreement, and provide information regarding WIC to the shelter. WIC outreach pamphlets and posters should be distributed and displayed in the shelter. The representative completes the Initial Evaluation of a WIC-Eligible Homeless Facility form (WIC #91). 7. After the orientation visit, the local WIC Program representative returns the completed Initial Evaluation of a WIC Eligible Facility form to the State Office. If the shelter is found to be able to comply, a letter will be sent from the Colorado Department of Public Health & Environment/WIC Program to the shelter and local agency, stating that the shelter is a fully-authorized WIC shelter. 8. A biennial (one time every two years) evaluation by a local WIC representative is required to ensure continued compliance with the Letter of Agreement and to allow an opportunity for further community outreach with the shelter. Shelters may receive an on-site visit or telephone contact at the discretion of the local agency. The

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 4: Organization and Management Revised: 03/01/2026

Page 2 of 2

Biennial Evaluation of WIC-Eligible Homeless Facility form (WIC #94) is to be completed every two years and a copy should be sent to the State Office within thirty (30) days of the evaluation.

Steps for Closing A Shelter The steps for closing a shelter are as follows: 1. Closure: Local agency forwards name and closure information for the facility to the State WIC Office for a facility that has notified them they are closed or plan on closing. 2. Termination: If the local agency has determined the facility is out of compliance based on a biennial evaluation or otherwise, the local agency will notify their assigned Nutrition Consultant. The State WIC Office will then work with the Local agency to make the final determination. 3. A Closure Letter will be sent from the Colorado Department of Public Health & Environment/WIC Program to the shelter and local agency, stating that the shelter is closed or terminated and shall refer all participants using such accommodation to any other accommodations in the area which meet these conditions.

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 4: Organization and Management

Revised: 01/01/2024

Page 1 of 2

Local Agency WIC Equipment and Inventory

Policy: Local Agencies shall purchase and maintain appropriate equipment to operate the Compass computer system.

Regulation: Office of Management and Budget Circular A-130, State Agecny and FNS Guidelines and instructions

Procedure/Additional Guidance: Computers Based on a predetermined schedule,the State office will allocate additional funding to elegible local agencies through a comtract amendment process for the purchase of new destop and laptop computers. The notification regarding eleigibility will be sent to the agencies prior ot the actual contract amendment. Local Agencies should work with their local IT department and collaborate on the specific needs required for WIC computers. Some specifics to be sure of before making computer purchases are:  Compatibility with Compaass: The new computers should be compatible with Windows 10, as Compass operates using this operating system.  Scanning Documents: When purchasing 64-bit computers, scanning documents within Compass requires a work around. Agencies need to scan the documents as black & white TIFF or JPEG files outside of Compass first andthen attach the files to Compass.  Anti-virus Software: It is recommended to use either McAfee or Norton for anti-virus software to ensure the security of the sytems.  Sufficient USB Ports: The new computers should have an adequate number of USB ports to acocomodate various periperhrals, such as mice, keyboards, signature pads, and magnetic stripe card readers.

The Local Agency WIC Program are instructed to follow their local agency policy when disposing of any computers and/or computer equipment.

All contract funds, including the computer funding, must be expended by the end of the current fiscal year. Unspent funds will not roll to the next fiscal year.

Multi-Function Printers The responsibility for the purchase of a multi-function printers lies with the local agency, if it is needed.

Magnetic stripe card reader The responsibility for the purchase of a strip card reader lies with the local agency, if it is needed.

Compass, the system used for WIC operations, requires the card reader device to present the card data as keyboard input. Therefore, a standard magnetic card reader device, such as one fo the USB-connected Magtek readers, will work seamlessly with Compass.

When considering which magnetic stripe card reader to purchase, the local agency must pay attention to the following critical specifications: 1. Card Format Compatibility: The card reader must be capable of reading ANSI/ISO/AAMVA car formats, ensuring that it can handle the standard formumats used for identification cards. 2. Keyboard Emulation Interface: The reader must provide a keyboard emulation interface, which means that when a card is swiped, the data from the card wil be transmitted to the computer as if it were being typed on a deyboard. Ths allows Compass to receive the card data and process it accordingly.

By selecting a magnetic stripe card reader that meets these specifications, the local agency can ensure seamless integration with Compass and smooth processing of card data for eQIC purposes.

Topaz Signature Pads The responsibility for the purchase of a Topaz Signature Pad lies with the local agency, if it is needed. The specific specifications for the signature pads and pens are as follows:

1. Topaz T-L755 Signature Gem LCD 4x3 pad (#T-LBK755-BHSB-R): This model is the Topaz Signature Gem LCD 4s3 pad. The model number is T-LBK755-BHSB-R 2. Topaz Signature Gem Series Replacement Pen (#P=ET110-HN): This is the replacement pen designed for the Topaz Signature Gem Series. The model number for the pen is P-ET110-HN

When purchasing these signature pads and pens, the local agency should ensure that they match the specified models to ensure compatibility with the system and smotth operation for capturing signatures electronically.

Inventory Local agencies that use WIC funds to purchase computer equipment, computer peripherals, television equipment and television should maintain a written equipment record for their records according to the Local Agency guidance.

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 4: Organization and Management Revised: 03/01/2026

Page 1 of 18

Local Staffing

Policy: Local WIC programs are required to have specific staff to carry out identified program functions and roles to ensure that local agencies are able to meet all program requirements and functions defined by federal regulations and state policy.

Regulation: CFR 246.11 c (7) (ii), CFR 246.2, CFR 246.6 b (2), USDA FNS WIC Nutrition Services Standards, FNS WIC Breastfeeding Curriculum: Peer Counselor Management

Procedure/Additional Guidance Staffing for the local WIC clinic includes the following positions/roles. Some staff may be in more than one position/role. ● Local Agency WIC Director ● Regional WIC Local Agency Director ● WIC High Risk Counselor (RD/RN) ● WIC Educator ● Local Agency Retail Coordinator ● Local Agency Outreach Coordinator ● Local Agency Breastfeeding Coordinator ● Lactation Management Specialist ● Educator WIC Lactation Specialist/Educator Advanced Lactation Credentials ● High Risk Counselor WIC Lactation Specialist/High Risk Counselor Advanced Lactation ● Designated Breastfeeding Expert ● Designated Breastfeeding Expert IBCLC ● Breastfeeding Peer Counselor Program Coordinator ● Breastfeeding Peer Counselor ● Breastfeeding Peer Counselor Lactation Management Specialist ● Non-WIC Staff with WIC Duties ● Volunteers

Local Agency WIC Director Local Agency (LA) WIC Director performs professional administrative and supervisory work in the planning, development, implementation and evaluation of the WIC Program. Oversees and coordinates the WIC activities of all clinic sites to ensure compliance with federal and state regulations. In large agencies, many of the duties described in this role may be delegated to other staff members. However, the ultimate responsibility for each duty falls on the WIC Director. In small agencies, the WIC Director and the WIC High Risk Counselor may be the same individual. The LA WIC Director works under the supervision of the agency's health officer or a designated high-level administrator. The LA WIC Director has line authority over subordinate professional and paraprofessional staff involved in the WIC Program.

Best practice is a dedicated 0.8 to 1.0 full-time equivalent (FTE) for this role.

Qualifications ● Education and Registration/License: The WIC Director must be a Registered Dietitian (RD) with the Commission on Dietetic Registration, a Registered Nurse (RN with a Bachelor’s Degree) licensed to practice in the State of Colorado, or a Medical Doctor (MD). Because WIC is a nutrition program, the position of WIC Director is ideally held by a Registered Dietitian. Note: In addition to the licensure requirements, a Bachelor’s Degree is the minimum education level required for this position. Preference is given to those who have a Master of Science (MS) or Master of Public Health (MPH) degree. ● Experience: Experience in public health or ambulatory care settings is preferred. A minimum of one-year experience in a public health setting or one year in a hospital setting is acceptable for consideration.

Knowledge, Skills and Abilities

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 4: Organization and Management Revised: 03/01/2026

Page 2 of 18

A fully functioning WIC Director should possess the knowledge, skills, and abilities listed below. In hiring for this position, supervisors should look for persons who possess most of these skills: ● Knowledge of human nutrition in health and nutrition needs for disease and its application to public health practices. Knowledge of nutrition needs for infants, children and women during the prenatal, postpartum, and breastfeeding stages. ● Knowledge of training, supervision, counseling, and educational concepts and methods. ● Ability to communicate effectively orally and in writing. ● Ability to manage Program operations and carry out Program planning functions; ability to formulate plans, policies, and procedures. ● Ability to organize, prepare, and analyze reports. ● Ability to establish and maintain effective working relationships. ● Ability to promote breastfeeding as the optimal infant feeding choice while allowing participant choice. ● Ability to supervise and direct professional and paraprofessional staff. ● Ability to develop forms and educational materials.

Responsibilities/Duties ● Completes the Colorado WIC New Employee Training program within the timelines defined. Manages overall WIC clinic operations: ● Formulates plans (including nutrition education plans), policies, standards, and procedures for the operation of the agency WIC Program within state and federal guidelines. ● Understands state and federal rules and regulations and follows up on agency deficiencies. ● Interprets and makes arrangements for implementation of federal and state regulations and policies. ● Evaluates implementation of new policies. ● Manages caseload and spending levels to meet appropriations by the State Office. ● Develops and makes recommendations for WIC budget proposals. Contacts State WIC fiscal officer and/or nutrition consultant regarding fiscal concerns/issues. ● Oversees, coordinates, and manages prescreening and waiting lists. ● Completes all forms/reports as requested by State WIC staff for monitoring and site visits; attends monitoring and site visit sessions; follows up on all monitoring findings and submits a timely response to the State Office. ● Ensures required retail monitoring and vendor training is done and that retailer monitoring reports are completed; works with retailers to prevent or correct problems. Ensures retailer contacts are documented in retailer files, and retailer misuse is documented in participant electronic charts. Ensures the State Retailer Coordinator is contacted with vendor problems/issues. ● Evaluates services to participants including clinic flow, use of staff time, clinic access, phone coverage, clinic space, and community needs. ● Provides the State Office with immediate feedback on adverse consequences of State policies or if policies are not understood. ● Ensures consistency among clinics in technical procedures and use of forms. Makes regular visits to all decentralized clinics to oversee operations. ● Oversees maintenance of equipment and testing for accuracy at all clinic sites. ● Maintains participant confidentiality and ensures that participants are treated equally and with respect, compassion, and empathy. ● Informs the State Office of major changes (i.e., staff, address, telephone, clinic hours which affect services). ● Participates in continuing education activities; attends meetings, conferences, and workshops; keeps abreast of current nutrition research as it relates to the WIC Program and participants. Registered dietitians must maintain registration with the required 75 credit hours per five-year period. ● Runs appropriate reports to verify food benefit issuance and redemption, processing standards, caseload management, etc. ● Contacts nutrition consultant with questions concerning caseload, management reports, clinic flow, State policies, equipment needs, nutrition education, staffing, and monitoring visits. ● Maintains a basic working knowledge regarding the Compass computer system and how it operates. ● Complies with the state WIC office regarding security, operations and functions of the Compass system. ● Ensures that administration areas of Compass are updated: referrals, pamphlets, Master Schedule, etc. ● Acts as LA Breastfeeding Coordinator (unless other staff is appointed).

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 4: Organization and Management Revised: 03/01/2026

Page 3 of 18

● Completes the WIC Lactation Specialist (WLS) Training to become WLS certified during the next WLS certification window ● Oversees breast pump loan program. ● Oversees Breastfeeding Peer Counseling (BFPC) Program (if applicable). ● Ensures staff is well trained. o Recruits, interviews, and recommends individuals for hire. o Oversees or conducts the orientation, training, and evaluation of newly hired WIC personnel. ✔ Ensures new staff complete Level I, II and III of the Colorado WIC New Employee Training Program as outlined by the state office. ✔ Observes staff interaction during appointments, including performing thorough nutrition assessments and providing nutrition information and counseling participants. o Defines staff roles and responsibilities, evaluates participant/staff ratios and staff needs. o Supervises WIC staff including annual performance evaluations, ongoing coaching and feedback. o Ensures continuing education opportunities for staff, including at least two sessions per year devoted to nutrition education. o Holds regular staff meetings to provide and enhance communication, to provide updates on policy and procedures, and provide staff training. Monthly staff meetings are optimal; however, small agencies may need bi-monthly or quarterly meetings. o Ensures quality nutrition education services to participants. o Develops or adapts and implements protocols of nutrition care. o Ensures staff members are trained in protocols. o Ensures that a WIC High Risk Counselor is available and trained to provide high risk education contacts. o Defines high risk for the agency (ensuring the State defined minimum definitions of high risk are covered); ensures WIC Educators know how to make appropriate referrals of high risk participants to the WIC High Risk Counselor. o Observes counseling skills of all staff members to ensure that accurate and appropriate information is being disseminated and that counseling skills are adequate. Trains staff in areas where improvement is needed. o Ensures that the documentation in participant electronic chart meets the required criteria listed in the WIC Program Manual. o Reviews, selects, or develops nutrition education materials as needed. o Attends and ensures that all staff members attend State sponsored WIC training. Attends and ensures that all staff members attend required State sponsored WIC trainings. o Recommends and registers staff for the WLS training (including suggesting staff take training as a refresher if staff completed the WLS training more than 5 years prior). o Oversees the implementation of Program nutrition objectives, participates in the nutrition education planning process via State Office guidance, and ensures that nutrition education and data collection conforms to standardized and accepted practices. ● Coordinates activities with other community services. o Arranges outreach and publicity for the agency WIC Program. o Develops formal referral relationships with pediatric and obstetric health caregivers. o Acts as a liaison to the community regarding WIC services, policies, and/or nutrition issues (e.g., informing and updating health care providers, social service agencies, assessing community needs). o Coordinates and assists staff to be familiar with community resources and services when referring WIC participants.

Partnership WIC Local Agency Director Partnership WIC Local Agency Director (PWLAD) performs professional administrative and supervisory work in the planning, development, implementation and elevation of the WIC program. Oversees and coordinates the WIC activities of multiple agencies/counties and clinic “satellite” sites to ensure compliance with federal and state regulations. The PWLAD may delegate some of the duties described in this role; however, the ultimate responsibility for each duty and all contract requirements falls on the PWLAD. The PWLAD works under supervision of the agency’s health officer or a designated high-level administrator and has line authority over subordinate professional and paraprofessional staff involved in the WIC program at all sites in the region. Roles related to the human resource management of staff at satellite agencies may remain a responsibility of that agency, depending on the structure and agreement between agencies and approved by the state authority.

Colorado WIC Program Policies and Procedures Section 4: Organization and Management Revised: 03/01/2026

Page 4 of 18

Best practice is a dedicated 0.8 to 1.0 full-time equivalent (FTE) for this role.

Qualifications ● Education and Registration/License: The WIC Director must be a Registered Dietitian (RD) with the Commission on Dietetic Registration, a Registered Nurse (RN with a Bachelor’s Degree) licensed to practice in the State of Colorado, or a Medical Doctor (MD). Because WIC is a nutrition program, the position of WIC Director is ideally held by a Registered Dietitian. Note: In addition to the licensure requirements, a Bachelor’s Degree is the minimum education level required for this position. Preference is given to those who have a Master of Science (MS) or Master of Public Health (MPH) degree. ● Experience: Minimum of five years’ experience in a public health setting is preferred. Minimum of two years’ WIC experience is required.

Knowledge, Skills, Abilities All knowledge, skills, and abilities included in the LA WIC Director description, plus: Ability to manage multi- agency agreements, training, staffing, and resource management.

Responsibilities/Duties All Responsibilities/Duties included in the LA WIC Director description and all agreed upon duties in the MOU between partnership agencies, plus:

WIC High Risk Counselors (RD/RN) The WIC High Risk Counselor performs professional and supervisory public health nutrition activities by delivering direct care participant services as well as participating in program planning and evaluation as assigned. In small agencies, this professional may be the same individual as the WIC Director. The WIC High Risk Counselor works under the supervision of the LA WIC Director and may supervise the WIC Educator and/or other WIC High Risk Counselors as assigned.

Best practice is a ratio of approximately 1 full-time equivalent HRC to 1500-1850 clients for this role, depending on other duties (supervision, clinic oversight, etc.).

Possible Titles: ● Nutritionist ● Registered and/or Licensed Dietitian ● Community High Risk Counselor ● Public Health High Risk Counselor ● Community Nurse ● Public Health Nurse ● WIC High Risk Counselor

Qualifications ● Education and Registration/License: The WIC High Risk Counselor must be a Registered Dietitian (RD) with the Commission on Dietetic Registration, a Registered Nurse (RN with a Bachelor’s Degree) licensed to practice in the State of Colorado, Medical Doctor (MD), or Physician Assistant (PA). Because WIC is a nutrition program, the position of WIC Director is ideally held by a Registered Dietitian. Note: In addition to the licensure requirements, a Bachelor’s Degree is the minimum education level required for this position. Preference is given to those who have a Master of Science (MS) or Master of Public Health (MPH) degree. o RD eligible allowed for a maximum of 6 months post hire date. ● Experience: Experience in ambulatory care, public health, or clinical setting.

Knowledge, Skills and Abilities A fully functioning WIC High Risk Counselor will need the knowledge, skills, and abilities listed below. In hiring for this position, a supervisor should look for persons possessing the majority of these skills:

WIC Educator The WIC Educator delivers WIC services to participants by determining and documenting eligibility, issuing food benefits, maintaining participant and Program electronic records and paper files related to participant certification, interviewing, providing nutrition education with behavior change goals, and developing individual care plans based on a sound understanding of nutritional concepts.

The WIC Educator develops proficiency in providing the full range of WIC services to participants. Titles of these individuals might include Lead WIC Educator, Administrative WIC Educator, WIC Receptionist, WIC Technician, WIC Clerk, or WIC Program Assistant. Lead WIC Educators are typically assigned higher-level duties such as training and supervising other staff.

The WIC Educator is expected to work under minimal supervision and to exercise independent judgment and a high degree of initiative within established procedures. The Educator works under the supervision of the WIC Director, WIC High Risk Counselor or designated WIC Supervisor.

Best practice is a ratio of approximately 1 full-time equivalent Educator to 400-500 clients for this role, depending on other duties.

Qualifications ● Because WIC is a nutrition program, the job of WIC Educator is ideally held by a Diet Technician (someone who has a two-year degree in nutrition science). Also highly desirable in this position is a Licensed Practical Nurse (LPN). All persons hired as a WIC Educator must complete the Colorado WIC New Employee Training Program modules within defined timelines. ● Education: Minimum high school diploma or GED. ● Experience: Previous work experience with the public. WIC and/or public health experience and experience with low income participants is preferred. ● Special Qualifications: Bilingual (Spanish) desirable.
